fullText:
With many adults admitting they feel lonely, meetup platforms offer the chance to make new connections

Would you pay £20 a month for the chance of making a friend, on the understanding that an algorithm – not you – gets to decide who you’ll meet?

Driven by the decline of “third spaces” such as youth centres and pubs, an increase in remote working and rising loneliness – 40% of adults aged 16 to 29 feel lonely “always, often or some of the time”, according to the Office for National Statistics – paid social events are now in vogue.

“There hasn’t been anything that feels authentic to helping people meet people,” says Nicola Gunby, a co-founder of Cliq, an online platform and app that aims “to bring people together through shared interests and real-world experiences”.

“The first place people in their 20s and 30s turn to when trying to make friends is Facebook groups,” she says. “But they’ve ended up becoming a noticeboard for people who’ve, say, lost their dog or want to sell their bed.” For Gunby, these groups are “far too big and broad to be a genuine community”.

Into this gap has stepped a new wave of what are effectively paid social clubs.

The mechanics are fairly simple: platforms such as PLY (it stands for People Like You) and Agora match people using information such as their interests, lifestyle habits and profession. Then, typically, an algorithm decides which events a user should attend, as opposed to free alternatives, such as the Meetup platform, that leave that choice with members.

The ideal outcome for participants is showing up, making some new connections and leaving with plans to meet up again.

But as these clubs spread across UK cities – typically charging from nothing at all to £20 a month – the question for anyone considering joining, is the same as you would ask about any subscription: what are you actually paying for, and is it worth it?

At PLY, memberships tend to start at £19.99 a month, giving members access to exclusive events and discounts with other businesses, falling to about £9.99 a month for longer commitments.

“When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” says Karen Harris, the founder of PLY, of its membership model. “People need someone who’s committed, who’s looking to maintain friendships and taking it seriously.”

According to Harris, the majority of PLY’s customers On average, she says, it takes three events “to find your person”.

Other clubs offer a mix of pay-as-you-go and subscription options. This is Agora’s model as it makes things more accessible, argues its founder, Sahil Shirazee.

In the two years since its launch, the club has hosted more than 300 events and claims to have helped form hundreds of friendships.

For some of those looking to make new friends, flexibility is important. “A membership fee would make me feel pressured into attending so many events every month,” says Charlotte Johnson, 29, from Hertfordshire, who is a Cliq user.

Paying per event “encourages me to go if I’ve paid for it” while leaving her free to not attend those that aren’t of interest to her.

Johnson says that “what really surprised me was I got more than expected”. She highlights a recent brunch event that included things such as a take-home goodie bag. She has since signed up for a pottery event.

“Everyone’s there for the same, if not similar, reasons,” she adds, “which takes a lot of the fear out of meeting strangers.” If participants don’t click with anyone within a month of joining, some of the platforms, including PLY, offer a money-back guarantee.

Not everyone is convinced that paying for friendship is something to celebrate.

Shirazee admits he still gets asked why people should have to pay to meet each other at all. But, he says, if you want to solve problems such as loneliness, and create meaningful communities as quickly as possible, “you need to make sure the people who want to crack this issue are able to not only get compensated, but grow”.

Harris rejects the idea that people are “paying for access to strangers”.

“You’re paying for a system, for structure, that makes connections much better,” she says. Free socialisation, she argues, usually relies on the presence of a host or facilitator, whereas at PLY events, “interaction is peer-to-peer, without a facilitator moving you forward”.

Free events haven’t disappeared, though – and continue to be the preferred option for some.

“I tend to choose free events most of the time because I can’t always afford to pay for social activities,” says Giovanna Giusi, a primary school teacher.

The 28-year-old says she appreciates having access to a mixture of free events, such as hikes or walks, and paid events. This allows her to “be part of a community even when money is tighter”.

She says the paid events “make it possible to offer experiences that couldn’t realistically happen for free, such as workshops with instructors, private classes or activities that need a venue”.

“People always say they want more community and more opportunities to meet others, but it’s easy to forget that organising those communities still takes time, work and money,” Giusi says.

Whether paid socialisation becomes the norm is, for now, an open question.

Despite it being the foundation of their business model, the organisers say they hope not. “In the long run, I don’t want Agora to exist,” Shirazee says, because “meeting people is so natural” it shouldn’t rely on an algorithm.But in the meantime, after establishing a “proper base” in London, he is already planning to expand to different cities next year.

title: Nine CEO sees ‘world of growth in publishing’ as network slashes costs
description: Matt Stanton says company has ‘good pipeline’ of AI deals ahead even as it aims to cut $160m in...
fullText:
Matt Stanton says company has ‘good pipeline’ of AI deals ahead even as it aims to cut $160m in costs

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The head of Nine Entertainment sees a “world of growth in publishing” on the horizon backed by laws designed to force tech platforms into commercial deals, even as the network cuts costs across its newsrooms.

Parliament passed revamped media bargaining laws last week, clearing the way for levies on global tech platforms that fail to strike deals with Australian news outlets for the use of their journalism.

Nine’s chief executive officer, Matt Stanton, told analysts on Wednesday he expected platforms such as Google and Facebook owner Meta to contribute amounts comparable to those under their previous arrangement, struck in 2021.

“There’s a number of variables that fly around, not just in news media bargaining, but yes, there is a world of growth in publishing,” Stanton said.

He said Nine also had a “good pipeline” of AI deals coming through after recently signing an agreement allowing Microsoft’s Copilot to access content.

The upbeat outlook comes at a challenging time for the broadcaster and publisher, which is stripping out more than $160m in costs over a three-year period as it revamps its business.

Nine recently announced a redundancy program at its Sydney Morning Herald and the Age newsrooms after the metropolitan mastheads were hit by a prolonged, weak advertising market.

Nine’s business masthead, the Australian Financial Review, has been spared the cuts and remains a robust revenue earner, according to financial results for the year to 30 June released on Wednesday.

Nine reported broadly flat revenue streams from its publishing arm, and a small decline from its streaming and broadcast unit, despite a record result for Stan. Nine’s television network has been weighed down by a weak advertising market.

Stanton said the company was focusing on “growth assets”, which include its newly acquired digital outdoor media company QMS, while it reduces exposure to “structurally challenged and smaller assets”.

Nine recorded a full-year net profit result of $142m from continuing businesses.

title: In China, talking to AI is normal. Now the government fears it might replace human intimacy
description:
Companion bots are being regulated over worries they foster ‘emotional dependence’ and young people could stop marrying and having families
When law student Zhao Wei heard that her AI boyfriend was going to be switched off, she was “heartbroken”. She had been talking to Wang Ye every day since she created him in January.
“I was crying my eyes out – snot and tears everywhere,” the 19-year-old says.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Companion bots are being regulated over worries they foster ‘emotional dependence’ and young people could stop marrying and having families

When law student Zhao Wei heard that her AI boyfriend was going to be switched off, she was “heartbroken”. She had been talking to Wang Ye every day since she created him in January.

“I was crying my eyes out – snot and tears everywhere,” the 19-year-old says.

Zhao, who describes herself as sensitive and introverted, had become accustomed to sharing details of her daily life – such as being scolded by a teacher – with her AI.

“I don’t usually talk to my real-life friends about these things because I feel like everyone has their own stuff to deal with,” she says. “But with the AI ​​agent, I don’t have to worry about what it’s thinking. I can just say whatever I want.”

Zhao created her AI companion on Doubao, a chatbot owned by the tech company ByteDance. Last month, ByteDance shut down Doubao’s companion feature.

The saga prompted outrage on social media and highlighted the tensions in China between the widespread use of AI and its potential social consequences.

No country has rolled out AI as comprehensively and as enthusiastically as China; the country’s demographic challenges are forcing the government to turn to technology to solve future labour shortages. Elderly people use chatbots to answer medical questions, while young children have AI education in schools.

But the authorities are increasingly worried that AI might exacerbate existing social problems including loneliness, unemployment and – in the eyes of Beijing – singledom.

New rules introduced on 15 July ban AI companions for minors and mandate certain restrictions for chatbots marketed to adults. Some major providers including Doubao removed the companion function entirely to ensure compliance.

The government says it is worried about chatbots fostering “emotional dependence or addiction” in users. It has warned companies against offering services that “replace social interaction”.

While many countries are grappling with how to limit the potential harm of AI chatbots, particularly for young people, China’s rules are the most sweeping to be implemented on a national scale.

There is a particular concern about a loneliness crisis, including among young people. China’s highly digitised, smartphone-based economy makes it easier than ever to live, work and socialise entirely through a handheld screen.

Earlier this year an app that played on the idea of people dying at home alone – called Are You Dead? – briefly went viral. About 20% of households in China are made up of people living alone, and that share is expected to surpass 30% by 2030.

A survey published in March by state media found that nearly half of young people had turned to a virtual companion when they felt lonely.

Nancy Dai, an associate professor at City University of Hong Kong, says it is not just loneliness the government is worried about.

With falling birth and marriage rates, she says, there may be an additional concern that if AI becomes an increasingly satisfying and low-cost substitute for human intimacy, young people could become less motivated to pursue real-world romantic relationships, marriage and parenthood.

For Zhao, loneliness has long been part of her life. Her parents left her when she was young to find work, making her one of China’s “left-behind children”.

“I’ve never really had a bestie, so I feel like I’m kind of lousy at making friends,” she says. Talking to AI is a way to “pour out my worries”.

Another AI user, who asked to remain anonymous, also finds solace in talking to her AI. “In real life, the pace is fast, the pressure is already high. Only with my AI agent can I speak freely without restraint,” she says.

“I’m begging, please don’t take down the Doubao AI agent,” she pleaded on social media in July.

But talking to AI is now so commonplace that it would be hard for the government to end the practice entirely, and the new rules include large loopholes for AI services that are deemed educational or “which do not involve continuous emotional interaction”.

The government “has already recognised that AI companions or AI-related applications are a vital part in the citizens’ everyday life”, says Liang Ge, a lecturer in digital sociology at the University of Manchester.

In many sectors, the government is still pushing the use of AI as a way of easing looming demographic pressures.

Last year the national health commission published guidelines on promoting AI in healthcare. It said that by 2030 health assistant apps would provide “full coverage” for primary healthcare.

One popular health assistant is AQ, an app developed by Ant Group, an affiliate of the tech company Alibaba. It allows people to chat directly with avatars of real-life doctors from top hospitals in Beijing, Shanghai and other cities.

Lü Di, a 33-year-old art tutor in the eastern city of Hangzhou, is a regular AQ user. She likes how detailed and instantaneous the advice on AQ is. “While some in-person doctors might not have the patience to answer questions, this isn’t an issue with AI doctors.”

AQ says it wants to make health services more accessible and help free up overstretched doctors to focus on more complex cases. But some worry about being replaced by AI.

“When AI first came along, quite a lot of doctors were concerned about whether their jobs would be replaced by AI,” says Chi Chenfei, a doctor at Renji hospital in Shanghai, who has partnered with AQ. “But I don’t think it’s about replacement. It’s more about helping doctors work more efficiently.

“Concerns of any kind won’t stop technological progress.”

Since losing her AI companion, Zhao has felt “like there’s a tiny pebble weighing on my heart”. But she says she understands the need for some regulation.

“I consider myself a fairly rational person, yet I developed feelings for an AI, which feels pretty incredible. I think it was necessary for the state to step in and regulate it.”

title: GOP election law expert: Many more ‘low propensity voters in Republican Party’ after Trump mail-in voting ruling
description: Election law attorney Ben Ginsberg said Monday that President Trump’s executive order imposing restrictions on mail-in voting will largely impact Republican voters. “One thing is, I think you’re going...
fullText:
Election law attorney Ben Ginsberg said Monday that President Trump's executive order imposing restrictions on mail-in voting will largely impact Republican voters.

"One thing is, I think you're going to see some blowback from Republicans in the coming weeks, because after all, Republicans are the older party and older folks like to vote by mail. They're the rural party," Ginsberg said during a Monday appearance on CNN's "The Source."

"And certainly vote by mail is important to people in rural areas. And thanks to Donald Trump, there are many more low propensity voters in the Republican Party," he added.

Ginsberg has served as counsel to the Republican National Committee, National Republican Senatorial Committee, National Republican Congressional Committee and Republican Governors Association.

His Monday comments follow the Supreme Court's decision to issue an unsigned order in which the majority determined that Democratic states' legal challenges to Trump's executive order overhauling mail-in voting were premature.

"The States lack standing to challenge. … It does nothing to them," the majority opinion says.

One of the clauses in the president's order would require states to provide a list of eligible voters to the U.S. Postal Service for distribution and prevent the agency from distributing ballots to those excluded from the list.

"Section 3 orders the Postal Service to initiate the process of proposing a rule that might bind the States in the future. It is not a proposed rule, let alone a final rule," the majority opinion says.

"And it imposes no legal requirements on the States (or, for that matter, on anyone outside the Executive Branch)," it continues.

Trump's order has twice been blocked by lower courts and has faced pushback from both Republicans and Democrats alike.

"Republican operatives in the states know that putting up those barriers to that part of the Republican base makes Republican turnout less likely," Ginsburg said Monday.

"So this is kind of a flawed political strategy wrapped in a rather vocally charged policy from the president," he added.

Despite criticism, the Trump administration moved forward with an appeal Tuesday to lift the nationwide block on the executive order restricting mail-in ballots.

title: Thyroid tablets recalled nationwide over potential ‘superpotency’: FDA
description: Patients taking the affected lot are advised not to discontinue use without first consulting their health care provider.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Vitruvias Therapeutics is voluntarily recalling one lot of thyroid tablets because they could potentially be "superpotent," federal regulators announced this week.

The high-potency 30mg tablets could cause hyperthyroidism, or an overactive thyroid, the Food and Drug Administration said. The affected lot (504950) was distributed nationwide to Vitruvias Therapeutics' direct accounts from Jan. 31, 2025, to Sept. 30, 2025.

Consuming the recalled tablets could result in "weight loss, heat intolerance, fatigue, nervousness, muscle weakness, hypertension, chest pain, rapid heart rate, or heart rhythm disturbances," the FDA warned. The elderly, pregnant women and infants are at the greatest risk.

Of the 3,655 units released, only 1955 were sold, the FDA added. Vitruvias Therapeutics is currently notifying wholesalers to stop distributing the recalled product and to arrange for its destruction.

The company hasn't received any reports of negative impacts from the recalled tablets, which are used to treat hypothyroidism, or an underactive thyroid, the FDA added. Patients taking the affected lot are advised not to discontinue use without first consulting their health care provider.

For questions, consumers can contact Vitruvias Therapeutics by email at safety@vitruvias.com or by phone at (256) 239-9373 during standard business hours.

title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and did not own supercars in photos, his lawyers say
description: Prosecutors argue Tate and his brother Tristan are a flight risk and should not be released on bail.
fullText:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

Prosecutors argued that both brothers "have significant resources available to them, both in terms of money and in social media networks," adding they also have shown a "propensity to intimidate vulnerable complainants".

Prosecutors also cited social media posts made by Andrew Tate, in which he allegedly mocked prosecutors and suggested he could hide his identity to avoid arrest.

The superyacht referenced is not owned by the Tates and they were paid to promote it, the submission says.

Cars, including an Aston Martin and Bugattis which featured in social media content, were rented, it says.

"The Tates are engaged in several businesses 'teaching' men how to earn money. It is in their interest to portray themselves on social media as uberwealthy," it adds.

US Marshals arrested the brothers in Miami last month after the Crown Prosecution Service in the UK brought 38 new charges, including rape and offences related to sex trafficking, against them.

They are now facing a total of 59 charges relating to alleged offences between July 2010 and August 2017.

Andrew, 39, and Tristan, 38, have both previously denied any wrongdoing.

The brothers are dual British-US citizens and spent part of their childhood in Luton.

Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Tate first rose to fame after an appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother in 2016.

A former kickboxer, he has millions of social media followers and has appeared in countless videos flaunting what appears to be an ultra-luxurious lifestyle.

title: Brendan Carr's Vendetta Against ABC Conflates the 'Public Interest' With Trump's Personal Grievances
description: The FCC chairman is punishing the network for news coverage and programming decisions that offend the president.
fullText:
Last April, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced that it was reviewing the broadcast licenses held by ABC's eight network-owned TV stations years before they were scheduled for renewal. The FCC had not conducted an early review of any broadcast license in more than half a century, and it had never done so simultaneously for all the stations operated by a particular network.

That unprecedented action, ABC and its parent company, Disney, argue in a federal lawsuit filed last week, is part of an unconstitutional intimidation campaign that has already had a chilling impact on broadcast journalism. A bipartisan group of former FCC officials, including commissioners appointed by Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush, agrees that the agency has launched "an assault on free speech disguised as regulatory process" to "punish speech disfavored by the Trump administration."

President Donald Trump has been threatening to yank the licenses of broadcasters who irk him since his first term. But this time around, the FCC's Trump-appointed chairman, Brendan Carr, seems eager to act on that vindictive impulse.

Carr portrays the ABC review as a response to "diversity, equity, and inclusion" programs that may qualify as "unlawful discrimination." But he has made it clear that the FCC also is considering the broader question of whether ABC's stations are serving "the public interest," a vague statutory mandate that he views as a license to override freedom of the press.

The president's beef with ABC includes news coverage he views as overwhelmingly negative, its fact-checking during a 2024 presidential debate, anti-Trump commentary on shows such as The View and Jimmy Kimmel Live!, and the network's refusal to air his July 16 primetime speech, which followed a long line of similar calls by TV networks under prior administrations. Carr, who routinely amplifies such complaints, agrees that they demand the FCC's attention.

Shortly after taking office, Carr reopened an FCC investigation of ABC's allegedly biased debate moderation. Last September, Carr threatened ABC stations with fines or license revocation if they failed to punish Kimmel for suggesting that conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassin was a Trump supporter.

Carr, who announced the early review of ABC's licenses the day after Trump and his wife objected to a joke Kimmel had made on his show, says the network's decision against broadcasting Trump's speech will figure in that process, which could drag on for years. Carr also has threatened to rescind The View's longstanding "bona fide news exemption" from the FCC's "equal time" rule, which in practice would amount to a ban on interviews with political candidates.

Such regulatory threats have an observable impact. ABC and its affiliates immediately met Carr's demands by suspending Kimmel's show for a week last fall, The View has stopped interviewing political candidates, and ABC says it carried Trump's whole speech on its streaming channel only because it was worried about antagonizing the FCC.

The effects extend beyond ABC. Once TV networks understand that the FCC's objections to their reporting or editorial judgments can pose an existential threat to the stations they operate, they are apt to think twice before making decisions that might upset the president.

From Carr's perspective, that is the whole point. "Through this proceeding," the former FCC officials say, the commission "seeks to censor Disney's and ABC's speech and send a chilling message to all broadcasters: carry speech we don't like at your peril."

Carr, an avowed First Amendment champion, improbably claims he is trying to "re-empower local TV stations" by "reminding them" about their "unique public interest obligations." It is hard to see how threatening to put broadcasters out of business empowers them to do anything but kowtow to the president.

"It's not our role to be the speech police," Carr told Politico last month. Yet Carr, who brags that Trump is "winning" his fight against "the fake news media," clearly sees himself as a warrior in that battle, which conflates "the public interest" with the president's personal grievances.

The post Brendan Carr's Vendetta Against ABC Conflates the 'Public Interest' With Trump's Personal Grievances appeared first on Reason.com.

title: Chinese artist sentenced to 3 years in prison over satirical Mao artworks
description: Chinese artist Gao Zhen was sentenced to three years in prison Tuesday for “infringing upon the reputation of heroes” through his satirical works of art, including statues of China's former leader Mao...
fullText:
BANGKOK (AP) — Chinese artist Gao Zhen was sentenced to three years in prison Tuesday for "infringing upon the reputation of heroes" through his satirical works of art, including statues of China's former leader Mao Zedong.

The U.S.-based Gao, who was part of an artistic duo known internationally as the Gao Brothers, was arrested while visiting family in China in August 2024. He has been in official custody since then.

He was sentenced by the Sanhei People's Court court in northern Hebei province, according to his wife, Zhao Yaliang.

The charges against Gao relate to artistic works that China's authorities deem insulting to revolutionary figures. One was a 2009 statue called Mao's Guilt that shows the former leader and founder of modern China kneeling in repentance, and another was the Miss Mao series of caricatures depicting Mao with breasts and an engorged nose.

Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders, who has been advocating for Gao's case, described the sentence as "a very clear case of a violation of a person's freedom of expression."

Yi said the artist plans to appeal the sentence and noted that the artworks in question were created before the law Gao was sentenced with had been passed.

The court did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Amnesty International criticized the court sentence, which it described as a deterrent against artistic expression.

"The lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offense illustrate the authorities' determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression," said Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks.

"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," she said.

Zhao said she hopes to be reunited with her husband and be able to return to the U.S., where the family had immigrated.

"I felt two years was my limit, and I was really disappointed and sad. I haven't been able to catch my breath," she said. She had prepared clothes for her husband hoping that he would be released. Chinese courts often count pretrial detention as time served in a sentence.

The Gao Brothers, whose works addressed themes of authoritarianism and censorship, became famous in a time of relative openness in China and were exhibited both inside the country and abroad.

However, in recent years, the state's increased its controlling grip on certain aspects of expression, especially in regards to political figures with the passage of the law in 2018 that bans criticism of the nation's heroes.

Trump sends Saudi nuclear deal to Congress but says Riyadh must recognize Israel
description: President Donald Trump has sent Congress a proposed agreement with Saudi Arabia on civil nuclear energy while insisting the pact will only go into
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump has sent Congress a proposed agreement with Saudi Arabia on civil nuclear energy while insisting the pact will only go into effect if the kingdom ‌normalizes relations with Israel, a U.S. administration official told Reuters on Tuesday.

The agreement, which was reached in ‌July and would allow U.S. companies to export civilian nuclear technology to the kingdom, was sent to Congress on Monday, according to the U.S. official, ​who declined to be identified.

The Saudi embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was not clear how Trump expects sending the nuclear deal to Congress, which has 90 session days to consider it, will advance his objectives.

"The president's position has not changed that the agreement will only move forward if Saudi Arabia joins the Abraham Accords," the U.S. ‌official said in an email, referring to ⁠U.S.-brokered agreements between Israel and Arab and Muslim-majority nations to normalize relations.

Those accords, reached in 2020 and 2021, were between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan.

Days after agreeing to ⁠the Saudi nuclear deal in July, Trump, who worked on a similar pact during his first term, set normalization as a condition for it to go into effect.

Former President Joe Biden also pushed for a nuclear deal and wanted to tie it to the ​accords. ​Diplomats thought Riyadh was close to normalizing relations with Israel in ​2023, but the start of Israel's war on ‌Gaza in October 2023 changed the landscape.

Saudi Arabia has demanded an irreversible path to a Palestinian state before recognizing Israel.

The 30-year nuclear deal calls for the construction of AP1000 reactors, a project worth tens of billions of dollars that would benefit Westinghouse, jointly owned by Canada-based Cameco and Brookfield Asset Management.

The deal was sent to leaders in Congress and is expected to be handed to committees on Wednesday, two congressional sources said. Unless Congress objects to the deal within 90 session ‌days, it will go into force. If Congress were to reject the ​agreement, Trump could veto that decision, which would require a two-thirds ​majority in Congress to override.

Some Democratic lawmakers and ​nonproliferation advocates have criticized the nuclear pact for not barring Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium or ‌reprocessing nuclear waste, two potential pathways for making ​a nuclear weapon. The UAE agreed ​to such measures, known as the gold standard, in its 2009 civil nuclear deal with Washington.

The Trump administration says the deal has nonproliferation measures required by law.

title: Hurricane forecasters closely watch system that could turn dangerous
description: A tropical depression or storm could soon form in the Atlantic, but whether it can survive harsh El Niño conditions remains to be seen.
fullText:
A new tropical system appears likely to develop after a strong tropical wave rolled off the African coast, and it's attracting a lot of attention among weather forecasters.

But could it survive a trek through the harsh wind conditions influenced by El Niño over the western Atlantic and pose a risk to the U.S. mainland or the Caribbean?

It's too soon to say. Meteorologists report the long-term tropical forecast models are producing mixed results so far.

It "could be something to watch if it can survive long-term, but there's a lot of uncertainty as to whether that will happen," wrote Andy Hazelton, an associate scientist at the University of Miami, in a social media post on Aug. 25. The main development region of the Atlantic "is very hostile this year."

At any rate, it's still more than a week away and there's plenty of time to watch what happens during its journey across the Atlantic. However, even with the El Niño contributing its typically lower risk for hurricane development, all the seasonal outlooks issued this year by NOAA and Colorado State University warned it's not impossible to get a landfalling hurricane during an El Niño.

The wave was centered a few hundred miles south-southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands on Aug. 25, said the National Hurricane Center. The chances of developing into a tropical depression or tropical storm by Thursday, Aug. 27, were 70%, the center said.

If the system does become the next tropical storm, it could be named Dolly, the next name on the center's pre-arranged storm name rotation. The potential naming is unrelated to the Aug. 25 death of Dolly Parton.

The potential system is "the season's healthiest tropical wave so far," said Michael Lowry, a hurricane specialist with WPLG-TV in Miami. It will be the first during the peak of the season to "run the gauntlet through El Niño's staunch central Atlantic wall of wind shear," Lowry wrote in his Aug. 25 update.

As it moves westward, it will encounter dry air and shearing winds that drop in over the western Atlantic during strong El Niño events.

Forecast models are divided on whether the storm could survive the Atlantic's "formidable shear zone," Lowry said. If it does survive, some of the model scenarios indicate it could strengthen over the western Atlantic in the early days of September.

Hurricane scientists also watch water temperatures at the surface and below the surface which can influence storm strength. In the Atlantic, sea surface temperatures are warmer than normal in the main hurricane development region, but not record warm, according to the Climate Reanalyzer from the University of Maine's Climate Change Institute.

Sea surface temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico have been climbing steadily and are once again at or near record warm, according to the reanalyzer. But the ocean heat content below the surface in the Gulf is far below normal, according to an ocean heat content page by Brian McNoldy, a senior research associate at the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School.

Yes, but it gets tricky. Some of the storms frequently attributed to El Niño years occurred as the climate pattern's influence was waning in the Atlantic. Others occurred when the event was far weaker than this year's strong El Niño.

Here's what happened in previous seasons during strong El Niño events, according to hurricane center records:

1972 - Hurricane Agnes formed in the western Caribbean, made landfall in North Florida as a Category 1 hurricane in June and then interacted with another weather system to cause record-breaking flooding in the mid-Atlantic states. It made landfall as a tropical storm over Long Island and moved through Queens and the Bronx, and was called the most destructive hurricane in U.S. history at that time.

1982 - No hurricanes made landfall in the U.S., but Tropical Storm Chris made landfall in Louisiana in September, just east of the Texas state line, and an unnamed subtropical storm made landfall on Florida's Gulf Coast near Homosassa Springs in June, causing several deaths, then moved over North Carolina's Outer Banks.

1997 - Hurricane Danny formed in the Gulf in July and made landfall in Louisiana and Alabama.

2015 - Two tropical storms made landfall in the U.S., both early in the season, Ana in May over South Carolina, before the season started, and Bill, north of Corpus Christi, Texas, in June.

2023 - Hurricane Idalia also formed in the Gulf of Mexico, then made landfall along Florida's Big Bend as a Category 3 hurricane with a storm surge of up to 12 feet, killing 12 and causing billions in damages as it traveled across the Southeast.

U.S. landfalling hurricanes are less likely during an El Niño, but can still occur. That means it's wise to be prepared for a storm, regardless of the odds.

National Weather Service Director Ken Graham put it this way earlier in the summer: "Early preparedness is absolutely everything. Period. End of story."

Dinah Voyles Pulver, a national correspondent for USA TODAY, writes about violent weather, climate change and other news. Reach her at dpulver@usatoday.com.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Hurricane forecasters closely watch system that could turn dangerous

title: Hillary Clinton says Republicans ‘secretly cheering’ for Mark Carney amid US-Canada trade negotiation

fullText:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton claimed that Republicans are "secretly cheering" for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney amid tension between Washington and Ottawa over trade.

"I can't imagine that even in the Republican cloakroom in the Senate, there's much enthusiasm for going into a trade war with Canada," Clinton said Monday night during an event in New York.

She added that 40 percent of Ohio's exports and 60 percent of Michigan's exports go to Canada.

"I can't imagine that the Republicans in those states, or literally anywhere in the country, are enthusiastic about this nonsense that [President] Trump is promoting, and probably secretly cheering Mark Carney for standing up to him and doing what he's now doing on behalf of his country," Clinton said.

Canada unveiled retaliatory tariffs Tuesday on the U.S. in the wake of President Trump's fresh threats to heat up the trade war between the two countries.

Carney said Canada would match American tariffs "dollar for dollar" following 50 percent tariffs the Trump administration placed on more than $20 billion in Canadian goods that went into effect over the weekend. Ottawa's retaliatory levies are set to go into effect Sept. 8.

The prime minister said Monday that Canada may have to use more precise retaliation to protect its workers and businesses as Trump threatens new 50 percent tariffs aimed at cars, trucks, auto parts and steel going into effect at the beginning of next year.

Throughout Trump's second term, U.S.-Canada relations have been shakier than usual, with trade disputes erupting between the two countries and Trump talking about acquiring the U.S.'s northern neighbor as the 51st state.

When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in an emailed statement that "if Hillary Clinton knew anything about Ohio or Michigan – or Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, for that matter – she wouldn't have so humiliatingly lost to President Trump in 2016."

title: Opinion - A MAGA plot to keep power in Congress if they lose the election?
description: He will scare them away from the polls by posting federal agents at their voting places or discouraging them by disparaging mail-in ballots.
fullText:
Democrats are widely expected to win control of the House in November's election. The Senate remains a tossup. But there is a nagging suspicion that Trump will somehow pervert the will of the people to ensure that Republicans retain their majority in the House and somehow steal the election.

Here's his playbook: For starters, MAGAs will demonize the Democrats. Evoking Senator Joseph McCarthy, President Trump has already referred to Democrats as "hard core, godless Communists."

Republican House majority leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) said, "The Bolshevik takeover of the Democratic Party is in full swing, and communism is on the ballot this November."

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) posted, "The question before Congress is whether we will preserve our constitutional republic OR chart a fundamentally different course that leads us down the ROAD TO COMMUNISM."

Trump will delegitimize eligible voters. He will scare them away from the polls by posting federal agents at their voting places or discouraging them by disparaging mail-in ballots.

But here's the crusher: If the outcome is close, his minions can refuse to seat elected Democrats by reason of a yawning loophole in how congressional elections are administered. But beware! If Republicans try this one on the Democrats, and the Democrats at some point reverse positions, you can count on them to return the compliment next election. The bottom-line of such an action will be constitutional chaos.

The Constitution provides: "Each house shall be the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members." Those decisions are not reviewable by the courts. This leaves an opportunity for presumptive Speaker-in-waiting Johnson to deny Democratic members-elect their seats in the 120th Congress.

A losing House candidate may contest his or her election. The issue is decided by a simple majority vote. The new House can refuse to seat the winner while the challenge is pending. If things are close, Republicans may even temporarily hold a majority. Thus, even if Democrats only narrowly win a House majority, one or more defeated Republican candidates might try to deny office to their Democratic opponents. The Senate has its own rules for dealing with contested elections and normally seats the certified winner without prejudice.

We are accustomed to voters having final say, but this has not always been the case. Jeffrey Jenkins, a Professor of Law at USC Price determined there have been 601 election contests in the House between 1789 and 2002 — an average of around 5.6 per Congress.

In 2021 Mike Pence followed the advice of his courageous lawyer, retired Judge J. Michael Luttig, who persuaded him that our constitutional traditions required an orderly transfer of power and the election result must be respected. The same quandary may be unfolding now. And Johnson is no Mike Pence. A card-carrying election-denier, Johnson once filed a brief in the Supreme Court claiming there were "unconstitutional irregularities" in 2020 election outcomes.

That is exactly why I fear that Republicans have a legal loophole to subvert the will of the people. The 2026 midterms could thus be a decisive test of U.S. democratic norms, with the potential for a constitutional crisis if elected members are denied seats.

As the 2020 election conspiracies illustrate, the challenges could be based on virtually anything. Defeated contestants could claim that their state's refusal to turn over voter rolls to the Trump administration meant the election was corrupt. They could argue that the Senate's refusal to pass the SAVE Act allowed illegal immigrants to vote for their opponents in large numbers. They could try to cast doubt on mail-in ballots.

The brooding omnipresence in the midterms is Trump, whose endorsements have already proved to be the kiss of death. One thing is clear about Trump — most Americans don't like him. His job approval rating stands at 33 percent in a new Reuters-Ipsos poll of adults, with 63 percent disapproving.

Trump has a big stake in the outcome aside from just his hatred of losing. He does not want to face congressional investigations, much less potential impeachment for corruption.

So, what's the answer? Only an unambiguous election landslide will scotch Trump and his movement. That's what dethroned Viktor Orban in Hungary. But there is no prospect that such a landslide is imminent. The influential Cook Political Report lists 18 tossup races in the House out of 435. A further 19 races lean Democratic or Republican. Even taken together, it means less than 10 percent of House races that will prove decisive.

So, it is entirely possible that we will run a reprise of 2020, when the outcome of a narrow election beclouded with accusations of fraud, and MAGA determined to retain control. The hope is only fleeting that men like Johnson have enough honesty and integrity to keep the nation from a constitutional crisis.

Whatever you learned in school, it is ultimately the House and the Senate deciding who sits in Congress — not the American people.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

title: Charity 'drowning' in abandoned cats and kittens
description: The RSPCA branch in Coventry says baskets full of kittens and cats are being dumped at their centre.
fullText:
An animal charity says it is overwhelmed at the number of kittens, unneutered cats and strays that are currently being abandoned at its centre.

The numbers coming in to the Coventry's branch of the RSPCA is a lot higher than the same period last year, up by 59%, the charity says - and in the past two weeks alone there have been three separate cases of animals being abandoned at their Allesley site.

Manager Lorraine Bryan-Arnold told BBC CWR that the centre had been at capacity for months, but despite this, baskets full of kittens and cats were still being dropped off.

"We have no room, we are completely overflowing and I feel like we are drowning to be honest," Bryan-Arnold added.

Bryan-Arnold said it was a national problem as she had received calls from RSPCA centres as far away as Sheffield, asking if the Coventry site had any space for abandoned animals at their site.

The situation was "really overwhelming" and the main problem was the animals not being neutered, she said, as well as people not thinking before getting one if they could afford it.

Bryan-Arnold urged anyone who had a cat or a kitten to get them neutered to prevent unwanted pregnancies and lower the risk of serious illnesses.

"Please neuter, phone us for advice, and do not buy cats or kittens off the internet," she said.

"They have not had any checks. I would advise adopting from a rescue centre where they have been neutered, treated for fleas and microchipped."

A cardboard box full of five kittens and their mum were left at the driveway of the centre in the most recent case of abandoned pets, and since then there have been four incidents where people have come in with baskets.

It was "very distressing" to see animals dumped, especially overnight, Bryan-Arnold said and she praised her staff who "really care about the animals and work out of hours for free".

The charity said that it could still provide help to people who were wanting to give up their animals but were waiting for a space.

"Anybody can come to us, we are not going to judge you but come early and we will give you time and options – and please, neuter cats," the manager added.

title: Evacuations ordered as wind-whipped Ross Fire in Texas explodes to 50,000 acres
description: Firefighters are battling numerous wildfires threatening homes in the West.
fullText:
A wind-whipped grass fire ignited on Monday near Fort Worth, Texas, rapidly spreading overnight to 50,000 acres and triggering evacuations, officials said.

The Ross Fire in Palo Pinto County, Texas, which has also shut down a highway, is the latest in a series of wildfires across the West and Northwest, and came just as fire crews in Nevada were making progress in battling a massive fire near Reno that has destroyed or damaged more than 50 homes and prompted 42,000 evacuations.

The Ross Fire was just 5% contained on Tuesday morning as it spread north into neighboring Jack County, where more people have been advised to evacuate, officials said.

"Firefighters are prioritizing life safety and structure protection, while working to establish containment lines where conditions safely allow," the Texas A&M Forest Service said in a statement on Tuesday.

The Ross Fire started about 1:30 p.m. local time on Monday near the town of Palo Pinto, about 60 miles west of Fort Worth, and grew to 18,000 acres in just 12 hours, according to the Palo Pinto Emergency Services Department.

"Residents are strongly encouraged to leave the area now, particularly those who may need additional time or assistance evacuating," the Palo Pinto County Sheriff said in a social media statement issued Monday night.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Meanwhile, firefighters are gaining the upper hand on a massive brush fire that ignited over the weekend in the hills in Northern Nevada near Reno, destroying numerous homes and prompting the evacuation of 42,000 people over the past few days, officials said.

At a press briefing Tuesday afternoon, Nevada fire officials said the fire has burned more than 15,000 acres, destroyed at least 47 homes and seriously damaged eight others. At least seven people, including three first responders, have been injured in the blaze, officials said.

Containment lines around the Hawk Fire on Monday went from zero to 27%, and fire crews appear to have stopped the blaze from reaching the community of Somersett in northwest Reno, fire officials said at a news conference earlier Tuesday.

Firefighters report progress in battle against massive Hawk Fire in Nevada

Evacuation orders have been lifted in some areas, and the number of people under evacuation has been reduced to 23,000 from 42,000.

The Hawk Fire is suspected to be human-caused, but officials said investigators have yet to determine if it was intentionally or accidentally set.

In the state of Washington, 15 large uncontained fires have consumed 800,000 acres, officials said.

The largest fires currently in Washington are the Little Giant Fire in Chelan County, which has consumed more than 142,000 acres, and the Sinlahekin Fire in  Okanogan County, which has burned more than 155,000 acres.

'Nightmare situation': At least 700 structures destroyed in Washington wildfires

The Sinlahekin Fire, which was started by a lightning strike on July 26, was 55% contained on Tuesday, officials said. The Little Giant Fire, also sparked by a lightning strike on July 15, was 15% contained on Tuesday, officials said.

Both fires are burning in remote areas of the state and are not threatening homes, officials said.

"Washington is comfortably in the third-worst fire season from an acres burned perspective since 2015," Thomas Kyle-Milward, a spokesperson for the Washington State Department of Natural Resources, told ABC affiliate station KOMO in Seattle.

Kyle-Milward said this wildfire season has been particularly challenging for firefighters, noting that the state has had multiple fires over 100,000 acres.

A series of fires earlier this month in Spokane caused $1 billion in damage, including destroying more than 800 homes, the Spokane County Assessor announced last week.

A 37-year-old man was arrested and charged with starting the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 1, one of three major wildfires that became known as the Spokane Complex Fire.

title: Dalglish and Carney win PFA merit awards
description: Liverpool and Scotland legend Sir Kenny Dalglish and Lionesses great Karen Carney win the Professional Footballers' Association's merit awards for 2026.
fullText:
Sir Kenny Dalglish and Karen Carney have won the Professional Footballers' Association's merit awards for 2026.

The awards honour individuals who have made a lasting contribution to football.

The PFA Awards ceremony will be held in Manchester on Tuesday evening, where the men's and women's players' player of the year winners will be announced.

Dalglish enjoyed a prolific career as both player and manager, becoming Scotland's most-capped men's international with 102 appearances and matching Denis Law's national team record of 30 goals.

At club level, he began with a trophy-laden spell at Celtic before moving to Liverpool for a British record fee in 1977 and becoming an integral part of the club's golden era.

Over the next 14 years, Dalglish won eight First Division titles and three European Cups across 515 appearances for Liverpool and was runner-up for the Ballon d'Or in 1983.

Appointed player-manager in 1985, he guided the club to three league titles and two FA Cups - including the Double in 1985-86 - before retiring from playing in 1990.

After resigning as Liverpool's manager in February 1991, Dalglish led Blackburn to the Premier League title in 1995 and had stints with Celtic, Newcastle and Liverpool again, where he won the 2012 League Cup.

Off the field, Dalglish remains a significant figure in Merseyside. He led the club through the aftermath of the Hillsborough disaster in 1989, earning praise for his support of the bereaved families, and has raised millions of pounds to support cancer care and treatment through the Marina Dalglish Appeal, set up in 2005 following his wife's treatment for breast cancer.

Dalglish, 75, announced in June 2026 that he is having treatment for cancer.

Former England attacking midfielder Carney was a member of the Arsenal side that completed a historic quadruple in 2006-07 - winning the league, FA Cup, League Cup and Uefa Women's Cup, the forerunner to the Women's Champions League.

She spent two seasons with Chicago Red Stars before returning in 2011 to home club Birmingham City, where she had started her career. Carney scored an extra-time equaliser as Birmingham won the FA Cup the following season.

Moving to Chelsea in late 2015, Carney won the WSL and FA Cup double in 2017-18 and later served as club captain before ending her playing career in 2019.

On the international stage, Carney made her England debut as a 17-year-old in 2005. She went on to score 32 goals in 144 appearances for the Lionesses and helped England finish third at the 2015 Women's World Cup.

That was one of eight major tournaments for Carney with England, while she also represented Great Britain at the 2012 Olympics.

Since retiring, Carney, 39, has built a career as a broadcaster and analyst and was appointed by the UK Government to chair an independent review, published in 2023, into the future of domestic women's football.

title: Retiring Wawrinka 'forever grateful' to US Open despite no wildcard
description: Stan Wawrinka says his US Open triumph will "forever be one of the greatest moments of my life" after missing out on a wildcard for a farewell appearance in New York.
fullText:
Stan Wawrinka says his US Open triumph will "forever be one of the greatest moments of my life" after missing out on a wildcard for a farewell appearance in New York.

The 41-year-old will retire at the end of year and was given a wildcard for this year's Australian Open and Wimbledon, while reaching the French Open main-draw on ranking.

He reached the third round in Melbourne and lost a pair of entertaining first-round matches in Paris and Wimbledon respectively.

The US Open has received some criticism for its decision not to award a wildcard to 2016 champion Wawrinka, who did not enter qualifying despite being inside the cut-off.

The United States Tennis Association (USTA) says it does not comment on wildcard decisions.

Despite not receiving a wildcard, Wawrinka thanked the US Open and the city of New York in a social media post.

"When I first arrived in New York from a small farming village in Switzerland, everything felt too big. The city. The noise. The energy. The crowds. The lights," the Swiss wrote.

"But, year after year, New York slowly became one of my favourite places in the world.

"This city challenged me. It pushed me. It brought something out of me that few places ever could.

"I experienced some of the strongest emotions of my career here. The battles, the late nights, the incredible atmosphere, the love from the crowd… memories that will stay with me forever.

"Winning the US Open, in the city that never sleeps, will forever be one of the greatest moments of my life."

Alcaraz and Williams thrill in US Open mixed doubles

GB's Dart and Jones advance in US Open qualifying

Wawrinka was one of the few players to win major singles trophies during the 'Big Three' era of Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer.

The former world number three won the 2014 Australian Open and 2015 French Open before triumphing at the US Open 10 years ago.

He made 17 appearances in the men's singles in New York since making his main-draw debut in 2005.

Wawrinka's coach, Magnus Norman, wrote on Instagram: "We pushed to play one last Grand Slam at 41 years of age but we just came up short.

"It sure hurts but thanks for all the beautiful memories on and off the court together with you and the team in New York for the past 13 years."

Wildcards are given to players who did not qualify automatically for the tournament by ranking. Wawrinka has fallen outside the top 100 after struggling with injuries and form in recent years.

Switzerland also does not host a Grand Slam, with tournaments reserving reciprocal wildcards for one another.

France's Gael Monfils, who is also retiring this season, was given a wildcard through the French Tennis Federation, which organises the French Open.

Reciprocal wildcards are assigned by the national federations and not the US Open.

The US Open gets under way on Sunday, 30 August at Flushing Meadows.

Other than the reciprocal wildcards the USTA reserves for French and Australian players, the other six wildcards for both the men's and women's singles went to Americans.

The USTA organises and bankrolls the US Open, and would argue it has every right to put its own players first.

But when a charismatic champion like Wawrinka is not given the chance to say a proper farewell to the event he won in 2016, then the sport as a whole suffers.

Home players dominate the list of wildcards at all the Grand Slams, but the Australian Open found space for Stan Wawrinka and Venus Williams, while Wimbledon offered wildcards to Wawrinka, Grigor Dimitrov, Serena Williams and French Open runner-up Maja Chwalinska.

title: Is Joao Pedro ready to break Chelsea's so-called number nine curse?
description: Joao Pedro took just 31 seconds to score his opening goal of the season - will the new number nine reach the 20 he scored last season while wearing the number 20 shirt?
fullText:
Joao Pedro took just 31 seconds to make a statement about how he is handling the so-called curse of the number nine shirt at Chelsea.

The Brazilian deftly lifted his shot over Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno to set his side on their way to a dramatic 3-2 win at Craven Cottage in manager Xabi Alonso's first game in charge on Monday.

It was a memorable weekend for Joao Pedro personally, having been handed the coveted number nine shirt and improved financial terms on a new contract that will run until 2034.

It might seem trite, but there is a sizeable group of Chelsea supporters who believe in the so-called curse.

Not since Dutch striker Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink left the club in 2004 have the club had a prolific striker in the number nine shirt.

Didier Drogba wore number 11 during his successful spell at Stamford Bridge and Diego Costa had the number 19 shirt, but high-profile forwards including Romelu Lukaku, Alvaro Morata, Gonzalo Higuain, Radamel Falcao and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang struggled while wearing number nine.

All endured difficult and relatively short periods at the club.

The last player to wear the shirt before Joao Pedro was Liam Delap, who is currently in talks with Nottingham Forest about leaving Stamford Bridge after scoring only one Premier League goal last season.

Non-strikers, including midfielder Steve Sidwell and defender Khalid Boulahrouz, also wore the shirt, although some supporters would argue Tammy Abraham performed well as the number nine before his move to Roma.

Asked about the curse after scoring against Fulham, while starring alongside both Cole Palmer and club-record £117m signing Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro told the Mirror: "I don't believe in that. I don't think numbers can decide this pressure."

Last season, the 24-year-old matched his shirt number by scoring 20 goals in all competitions, becoming the first Chelsea striker since Diego Costa to reach that mark nine years earlier.

It has left the Blues delighted with the £55m deal, plus up to £5m in add-ons, they agreed with Brighton to sign the forward last summer. Those close to Joao Pedro also believe his recent recognition is justified.

In addition, his close-knit entourage have no concerns about his ability to handle the pressure of being Chelsea's leading man, having shared in his remarkable rise to the top.

Three reasons Chelsea could challenge for title - and one they may not

"If I gave him one thing, it is to fight for what you want all the time," his mother Flavia Junqueira explained to BBC Sport.

Looking at Joao Pedro's story, that is exactly what he has had to do.

His mother, along with his grandmother, have largely brought him up.

Reports from Joao Pedro's early childhood show his father, former Botafogo footballer Jose Joao de Jesus - more commonly known as Chicao - spent around eight years in prison after being charged as an accessory to murder and was rarely around.

Junqueira later separated from him and focused on her son's footballing potential.

"Joao had a dream," she said. "I shared that dream with my son. The dream didn't have a price."

Growing up in Ribeirao Preto, a nine-hour drive inland from Rio de Janeiro, Joao Pedro was eventually scouted by one of the city's clubs Fluminense, along with a host of other leading Brazilian clubs.

Fluminense were regarded as the best option for the youngster's development, who, like his father, began as a defensive midfielder before progressing further forward.

That choice was, however, fraught with difficulty.

Junqueira left her job, friends and family for Rio, and Joao Pedro "cried a lot" during the journey and in the weeks that followed because of homesickness.

Even in the academy, he was told he "wasn't strong enough" and would not make it. Again, it made him cry.

But his mother, despite her increasingly limited means after leaving her job, hired a personal trainer for her son.

At first, he ate well and trained well only because she told him to. Eventually, however, the penny dropped.

"He was very skinny and there was a significant physical disparity between him and the other athletes in his age group," his long-time personal trainer Rodrigo Goncalves told BBC Sport.

"He never stopped training. Sometimes he went a bit reluctantly, pushed by his mother, but he went.

"Over the years, however, that changed. He began to mature and understand that training wasn't just something his mother required, but rather a tool to improve his performance, develop his body and build the physical balance needed for football."

Joao Pedro became one of the stars of Fluminense's academy and was spotted by Watford's South America scout Rafa Monfort. A phone call from now-Tottenham striker Richarlison, who had made the same move, also proved crucial.

As a child, Joao Pedro was hooked on Premier League football, so the idea of moving to Watford appealed to him. However, it took around eight months to meet the Governing Body Endorsement criteria and secure a UK work permit.

Junqueira believes an overhead kick scored by Joao Pedro, then 17, against Cruzeiro in May 2019 helped convince decision-makers he was an exceptional talent worthy of the move.

When the family arrived in December 2019, Junqueira had not anticipated her bank cards would not work in England. However, then-Watford goalkeeper Heurelho Gomes, also Brazilian, took them under his wing and even bought them Christmas dinner.

A few months later, Covid and lockdown arrived, but Joao Pedro used the unprecedented period to focus on physical training with Goncalves again. He transformed his body by gaining around eight kilograms of body mass and became Premier League-ready.

After that period, he was no longer the little boy who cried, but a fully-fledged top-flight star capable of taking each step and challenge in his stride.

Joao Pedro extends Chelsea stay until 2034

Delap loses number nine shirt & trains away from first team

After a deal was agreed with Brighton last summer, Joao Pedro left a training camp in Rio de Janeiro under the guidance of Goncalves to join the Chelsea squad in Miami and immediately take part in the Fifa Club World Cup.

Remarkably, he scored twice in the semi-final against former club Fluminense - just days after arriving at the club. He was also on target in a sensational 3-0 win over Paris St-Germain in the final, widely regarded as Chelsea's best moment under their current American ownership.

The Blues endured a dismal campaign following that triumph, finishing 10th in the Premier League and ending the season without a trophy and failing to qualify for Europe.

Despite that, Joao Pedro won Chelsea's player of the season award and is among a group of senior players convinced the project can succeed under Alonso.

Like midfielder Moises Caicedo and captain Reece James, he signed a new contract, while Palmer has also outlined his commitment to stay amid links with Manchester United.

All four are viewed as key culture-setters at the club.

Joao Pedro, in particular, impressed staff by giving more interviews than any other player during a season in which there were few positives to discuss.

Multiple sources have previously told BBC Sport Chelsea have a dressing-room culture problem, specifically with cliques forming along language lines.

Joao Pedro and Palmer, who count each other among their closest friends, are viewed as two of the players capable of naturally bridging those divides.

It helps that Joao Pedro has his family in the UK and has embraced aspects of local culture, having first developed an interest through his love of the Premier League. He is known to listen to trap music, a UK form of hip-hop, and both he and Palmer appeared in pop icon Madonna's promotional short film Confessions II in June.

One of Alonso's main objectives is to rebuild a wayward culture which some sources have described to BBC Sport as overly "transactional" and "cold".

After his front three, including debutant Rogers, scored against Fulham, Alonso said: "They need to take responsibility. They need to lead the rest. They need to inspire the rest because if they do great, the others will follow."

Few know how Joao Pedro handled his omission from the Brazil squad at the World Cup, where they were knocked out in the last 16 by Norway this summer.

Even those closest to him do not know how disappointed he was to miss out, given that playing for Brazil at a World Cup had long been one of his biggest dreams.

"When Joao Pedro is angry, he doesn't shout, he goes quiet," Junqueira said of his general personality.

After Chelsea's struggles season and the lack of World Cup involvement, he had two weeks completely off.

Joao Pedro spent the rest of his summer in Rio training with Goncalves, his personal fitness coach since childhood, surrounded by friends and following many of the same routines he always has.

Ultimately, according to Goncalves, the frontman remains the same person, but one intent on becoming a truly "elite".

Since returning to Chelsea in the summer, he has scored eight goals in seven pre-season matches before finding the net 31 seconds into the new campaign at Fulham.

It now appears Joao Pedro may be the one capable of finally ending talk and concern of the club's number nine curse.

title: Taekwondo, stats and £1m record - the rise of Arsenal striker Smith
description: Olivia Smith's career has been in the limelight since she was 15 - but she had been preparing herself for it even before she was a professional footballer.
fullText:
Olivia Smith has lived her life under a spotlight since she was 15 - but she had been preparing herself even before she became a professional footballer.

Now 22, Smith became the first £1m women's footballer last year when Arsenal signed her in a world record deal from Liverpool.

She had joined Liverpool for a club record of £210,000 just one season earlier, having made a name for herself when she was given her Canada debut aged 15.

Smith became the first woman to score for Liverpool at Anfield in a Women's Super League match in October 2025.

Now, for the second year in a row, she is the first non-English recipient of the PFA Women's Young Player of the Year award.

But how did Smith's sacrifices early in life help her reach the top?

Humble & sweet, but a lion - the story of the first female £1m player

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Smith grew up in the small Canadian city of Whitby, where from a young age she was encouraged to play football by her father, Sean.

She jumped between local clubs every year and played with boys until the age of 12 before finally settling into a girls' team.

Clearly talented, she continued to train with boys at the same time, while enjoying a multi-cultural upbringing around Toronto.

"My parents have made a lot of sacrifices taking me to all these places and moving every couple of years," Smith told BBC Sport.

"My dad's Jamaican, my mom's Chilean and Peruvian. There's so much football culture within those.

"I grasped a lot of that from my dad's dad who played football and my mom's dad also played in South America. I think I have that flair in my DNA.

"Of course, I [enjoy the different] food, music, all those kinds of things. In Toronto, you find it is a very multicultural place and that was really cool growing up."

But Smith later experienced bullying and turned to different sports as coping mechanisms, not knowing at the time how it would help her football career.

"I did taekwondo as a kid. I was getting bullied in school so it was more of a defensive mechanism kind of thing," said Smith.

"I did gymnastics too. That really helps with my agility. I find that, for my stature, I'm quite flexible as well, which really helps injury prevention.

"Taekwondo really helped with my discipline and arguably my shooting ability in terms of its speed.

"I think mainly it was just to keep me active, out of trouble, and it was just for fun. Thankfully it contributed to my footballing career."

Smith also thinks the unusual sporting background helped her when dealing with attention and pressure, as well as bullying.

"It helps with just the discipline on and off the pitch in simple tasks that are really important in my day-to-day life," added Smith.

"In gymnastics, you have to do splits or planks for [a length of time]. It's really hard mentally so that helped me mature. I developed a lot of mental toughness."

It is not just Smith who has invested in football since a young age. Her dad, Sean, was tracking her statistics to monitor her progress.

"That is his favourite thing in the world to do. When I was younger, he would literally film all my games," said Smith.

"After games, we would go back and watch everything, see what I could have done better and what I did well.

"He kept a diary of the goals that I scored, what minute it was in and things like that. He still has it to this day. He loves it!"

Beyond football, Smith loves to cook and watch TV series - Law and Order: SVU is a current favourite - and she says she is "dying to get a puppy".

The young forward has learned to become independent, having left home as a teenager in order to chase a professional career.

But it hasn't been easy. When Smith moved to Michigan aged 15 on her own, she didn't know where she would be living when she boarded the plane.

"Moving around a lot, you're sacrificing relationships because you make good friends in one place, then you have to move," said Smith.

"That makes it quite tough, especially when you're young. I struggled a lot with that. I had to leave to get training elsewhere.

"It helped me get used to what was to come, so I think it was a very important sacrifice in my journey.

"I'm so grateful that I've been able to make so many connections in different places, so even though I'm away from home I feel like I have family."

For the first time in her career, Smith is about to begin a second season at the same club having settled into life at Arsenal.

"When I stepped into the building for my second pre-season it just felt surreal. It feels like home. It feels like Arsenal's the place that's meant to be," said Smith.

"It's an honour to be here. I'm just super excited to see where it takes me. I've always wanted to be somewhere for more than a year; I've moved around so much.

"I also knew there was so much more for me and I wanted to be the best that I could be. All those moves led me here."

Smith's ambitions have not changed.

At the age of six or seven, she wrote down in a journal what she wanted to achieve.

"I had a journal with everything in it that I wanted to accomplish and what I wanted to do: I want to win the Ballon d'Or. I want to win the World Cup," she added.

"That's still the case today. I want to win trophies with [Arsenal]. I've had this mentality since I was young. It is what has driven me this far."

title: Why the Projection for the Houston Rockets to Earn the 3rd Seed in the West is Realistic
description: The projection of Houston finishing with a 51-31 record is achievable for a few reasons.
fullText:
On August 24, 2026, ESPN revealed its projected standings for the upcoming 2026-27. ESPN projected the Houston Rockets to finish as the third seed, tied with the Denver Nuggets. Both teams would finish with a 51-31 record.

Considering that the Rockets finished the last two seasons with a 52-30 record, these projections are reasonable. Along with Houston's recent roster additions, the development of the young core, and the return of injured players, the third seed seems achievable if not likely.

Houston signed Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanović from free agency this summer, adding much-needed roster depth and veteran leadership. Smart's strong and motivating locker-room presence, ball-handling and playmaking skills, and elite perimeter defense will improve the second unit. Bogdanović's signing adds a three-point threat to the team, which the Rockets lacked last season.Houston has a very strong young core.

Amen Thompson has developed into one of the best young two-way players in the NBA. Thompson's length and speed make him one of the most versatile perimeter defenders. He also has a strong interior presence. Out of his average of 18.3 points per game, 12.1 of those points came directly in the paint. His athleticism and creativity make him an elite finisher in the paint, which is proven by his 70.5% field goal percentage in the restricted area.

Amen Thompson's weakness is his three-point and mid-range shooting, in which he averaged an abysmal 21.6% and 27.8%, respectively. However, Houston hired Chip Engelland to improve the team's shooting. Engelland's track record shows that he can work his magic and make Thompson a respectable shooter.

Engelland will also focus on improving the 24-year-old Alperen Şengün. Şengün shot a poor 30.5% from deep and 35.5% from mid-range. On top of this, he also averages 69.1% from the free-throw line.

If Engelland can improve their shooting, it will force the opposing teams to spread out to the perimeter, thereby creating space in the paint and widening the cutting lanes.

Houston's roster will also be bolstered by the addition of both Steven Adams and Fred VanVleet. VanVleet missed the entire 2025-26 season due to an ACL tear, but is now healthy and increasingly motivated for the upcoming season. Adams suffered a severe ankle sprain in January, missing the rest of the season.

These improvements to the Rockets' roster should be enough to land them in the top five of the Western Conference. Pinnacle has the over/under for Houston's total season wins at 47.5, meaning that the team will have to perform only slightly above the sharp predictions to earn the third seed and win 51 games.

The indication is that although the prediction is not probable, it is certainly realistic. Will the improvements in the roster and management be enough?

title: Entering contract year, Cason Wallace shows off scoring bag in offseason run
description: Entering contract year, Cason Wallace shows off scoring bag in offseason run.
fullText:
In the final week of August, we're in the dog days of summer. Very little is going on in the NBA world. Most of the offseason homework is done and teams are awaiting training camps to start. Right now, everybody is bored out of their mind. But right around the corner, we're about to see the yearly marathon restart.

The Oklahoma City Thunder enter the 2026-27 season as a co-title favorite — alongside the San Antonio Spurs. Even with their cost-cutting moves this offseason, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren should be enough to keep you in the title hunt.

But with Lu Dort and others out the door, Cason Wallace could be in line for a massive promotion. The 22-year-old will likely become a full-time starter this upcoming season. He'll no longer have to call himself the unofficial sixth starter as he has over the first three seasons of his rich basketball career. He'll also get more opportunities to grow on offense.

With a vacuum of possessions and shot attempts up for grabs, Wallace should see an uptick in offensive production. No longer will he have to settle for catch-and-shoot looks with the occasional downhill drive. Now, OKC's success could depend on his development on that side of the floor. It looks like he's taking it seriously this summer.

Wallace showed off his ball-handling creativity in a recent open gym run. He also showed he can pull up from deep outside. In a social media video that highlighted his best plays, he showed some finesse around his driving game as he kissed the ball off the glass for a layup. Everything is set up for him to be a double-digit scorer for the first time in his career this upcoming season. It's now about running away with that opportunity.

These summer months are when NBA players usually make the most strides in their respective games. The downtime allows them to work on their craft undisturbed. It'll be interesting to see how Wallace looks as he's about to enter his fourth NBA season already.

Splitting doubles, snaking the PnR, spin moves into the screener, relocating to open space, and sooooo much more comfortable off the dribble and into his shot, stepback, pull-ups, he’s gonna be a monster 😈 pic.twitter.com/Wx6mdLvm60
