title: 10 observations from Eagles’ open training camp practice at the Linc
description: Riq Woolen’s two interceptions, DeVonta Smith’s return and creative formations highlighted the Eagles’ open practice at the Linc
fullText:
Philadelphia always supports the Eagles Autism Foundation, and the festivities continued on Tuesday as more than 45,000 fans attended the annual open practice at Lincoln Financial Field. They were treated to several explosive offensive plays, two defensive touchdowns and another competitive training camp session.

Riq Woolen produced the biggest performance of the night, while DeVonta Smith showed why his return changes the outlook for Philadelphia's offense. Jalen Hurts experienced some encouraging moments and costly mistakes during an uneven performance.

Here are 10 observations from Tuesday's practice.

Woolen's status as a starting cornerback has never been in question, and Tuesday demonstrated why Philadelphia signed him to a one-year, $15 million contract. Woolen intercepted Hurts twice. He undercut a dig route intended for Makai Lemon on the first takeaway, then jumped an out route to Smith during a two-minute drill and returned it for a touchdown.

His length, closing speed and ability to recognize route concepts give Philadelphia another potential playmaker opposite Quinyon Mitchell.

Riq Woolen taking it to the house after picking off Jalen Hurts 👀 pic.twitter.com/1O32LzwQNR

Hurts generated several touchdowns and explosive completions, but his two interceptions prevented the performance from being considered a successful one. The first turnover came on a late throw over the middle. Hurts threw the second interception off his back foot while facing pressure from Jalyx Hunt. Woolen anticipated the out route and finished the play in the end zone.

Hurts also underthrew Smith on a deep post that could have resulted in a touchdown.

That after practice work Jalen Hurts and Hollywood Brown been putting in is showing #eagles pic.twitter.com/o9hR6W4TDx

Smith caught passes on a deep out and a play-action rollout during the first move-the-ball period. He later wrestled away a deep crossing route against tight coverage from Mitchell and accelerated toward the end zone. Smith also adjusted his angle on a dig route when Woolen attempted to undercut it. The route prevented Woolen from producing another takeaway and allowed Smith to turn upfield for a potential touchdown.

There were imperfections, including a drop on a third-down crossing route, but Smith's movement and explosiveness were encouraging.

Nice throw from Jalen Hurts to DeVonta Smith#FlyEaglesFly #NFL pic.twitter.com/xsUUFDR4xH

Philadelphia used Lemon out of the backfield during a red-zone period. The rookie ran a wheel route along the left sideline and was left uncovered for a touchdown. Dallas Goedert also aligned as an offset H-back, another indication that Mannion plans to use multiple players in fullback-style roles. The Eagles do not have to carry a traditional fullback if Goedert, Barkley, Lemon and other skill players can execute those responsibilities through formations and motion.

An easy TD for Makai Lemon pic.twitter.com/ziDNKask0L

Hunt overwhelmed Fred Johnson after Lane Johnson left practice and Markel Bell was unavailable. His pressure also contributed to Hurts' second interception. The third-year edge rusher has spent the summer establishing himself as a legitimate starter. Tuesday offered more evidence that his combination of length, speed and developing pass-rush technique can become a problem for opposing tackles.

Landon Dickerson received a scheduled rest night, allowing Drew Kendall to work at first-team left guard. Lane Johnson walked off with a trainer and remained on the sideline for the remainder of the competitive periods. Fred Johnson replaced him at right tackle and surrendered consecutive pressures during one series. With Bell sidelined by thumb and leg injuries, Philadelphia was forced to reach further into its offensive tackle depth. That move provided the clearest reminder of why reserve offensive line jobs are so important.

Lemon's most impressive moment came when he aligned at running back and caught an uncontested wheel-route touchdown. The formation displayed how Mannion can manufacture favorable matchups for the first-round pick.

The rookie was also the intended receiver on Woolen's first interception, providing another example of the timing Lemon and Hurts must continue developing after the receiver missed significant practice time with a hamstring injury. The Eagles are finding different ways to get the football into Lemon's hands. That may matter more than assigning him to a single traditional receiver position.

Barkley juked Baun during the first move-the-ball period and broke into the open field for a substantial gain.

His best receiving play came in the red zone when Hurts placed a wheel-route touchdown over Barkley's outside shoulder. Baun had strong coverage, but the placement and catch were too precise to defend. Philadelphia has continued looking for ways to feature Barkley as a receiver in Mannion's offense.

Jalen Hurts TD pass to Saquon with Zack Baun trailing in coverage. pic.twitter.com/Q7qdCiMiCn

Mitchell broke up the underthrown deep pass intended for Smith. Jihaad Campbell disrupted a throw to Lemon, while Woolen produced the two interceptions.

Philadelphia's offense created explosive plays, but the defense consistently challenged receivers and punished Hurts for poor ball placement. That competition should benefit both units as the Eagles approach the regular season.

Dalton received the first repetitions behind Hurts, continuing a pattern the Eagles have maintained despite Tanner McKee's stronger preseason production.

Dalton badly overthrew Darius Cooper early but recovered to throw a touchdown pass to Elijah Moore.

The depth chart order indicates that the competition remains open. Friday's preseason finale against Cincinnati will provide both quarterbacks with their last game opportunity to influence the decision.

This article originally appeared on Eagles Wire: 10 observations from Eagles' open training camp practice at the Linc

title: Football safety remains focus as new CTE study released
description: As football season kicks off for Durham Public Schools, athletic leaders are taking steps to keep student-athletes safer.
fullText:
As football season gets underway for Durham Public Schools, safety remains a top concern as researchers continue to learn more about chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE.

CTE is a brain disease linked to repeated head impacts.

"It's a progressive neurodegenerative condition that comes from sustaining repeated blows to the head over time," neurologist Leah Croll said.

A new study found that at least 25% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE. Croll said head impacts do not have to result in a concussion to increase the risk of developing the disease.

"They can be what we call sub-concussive hits," Croll said. "Over time, having more and more instances where you're hit in the head, that can contribute to increasing your risk for developing this condition."

Advocates described the study as a "sobering reminder that football carries real risks."

In a statement to ABC11, the NFL said the league "continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts."

CTE can only be diagnosed after death, meaning research has relied heavily on brains donated by players and their families. Researchers say that limitation makes it difficult to fully understand how the disease develops and how it can be prevented or treated in living people.

"It really slows down our research efforts when it comes to prevention and treatment of CTE, and that's a huge problem, particularly when it comes to kids," Croll said.

The study comes as a 17-year-old high school quarterback in Wisconsin died after suffering an on-field injury during a game.

"Any time a student-athlete loses their life or suffers a severe head trauma is concerning to everyone," Durham Public Schools athletic director David Hackney said. "We try to take every safety measure to try to prevent those things from happening."

Durham Public Schools uses Guardian Caps, soft-shell padding worn over traditional football helmets. Hackney said the equipment has helped student-athletes.

"I think Guardian Caps is a big step, but we can take it a step further," Hackney said.

Hackney said licensed professionals are also on-site at Durham football games to evaluate injuries. After an injury, an athletic trainer assesses when it is safe for a student-athlete to return to action.

"We monitor concussion protocols," Hackney said. "Our athletic trainers do an awesome job of making sure they're following up with the student-athlete, as well as their parents, to make sure that they're following all those safety measures and that they take every precaution before they are allowed back on the field."

School officials said those measures are intended to reduce risks and help protect student-athletes throughout the football season.

title: Reachpad CLI – Spin up free sandboxes in seconds to develop apps
description: The reachpad CLI: workspaces where Claude, Codex and other coding agents build full-stack apps and share them by link, from your terminal. - Reachpad/reachpad-cli
fullText:
Run coding agents in durable cloud workspaces: disk and memory survive the
machine underneath, so a paused workspace resumes mid-session.

With Homebrew on Apple silicon macOS or x86_64/arm64 Linux:

With npm, anywhere Node 18+ runs:

Or with the checksum-verifying installer:

Linux x86_64/arm64 (musl, static) and macOS arm64/x86_64. The script fetches
the latest release from this repository, verifies its checksum against
SHA256SUMS, and installs to ~/.local/bin/reachpad (override with
REACHPAD_INSTALL_DIR).

All three deliver the same binary. @reachpad/cli is a launcher around it, not
a second implementation — see npm/README.md, which also
explains the macOS quarantine problem npm sidesteps.

On first use, the CLI shows a short code, opens WorkOS hosted sign-in, and then
lists your workspaces. WorkOS handles the account login and any required MFA or
SSO. After approval, Reachpad exchanges the short-lived WorkOS token once and
saves a user-scoped Reachpad credential and the production endpoint with mode
0600. No password or authentication factor is entered into Reachpad.

On a remote machine without a usable browser, run reachpad auth login --no-browser and open the displayed URL on another device. The manual
credential flow remains available from
reachpad.dev/connect as a recovery path.

Then list, create, or attach to a workspace:

reachpad update respects how Reachpad was installed: Homebrew installs are
directed to brew upgrade reachpad and npm installs to npm install -g @reachpad/cli@latest, while installer-managed binaries are updated in place
after the release checksum is verified. Whoever installed the binary owns it —
a second writer is how a working install becomes a broken one.

This repository carries the full CLI 
binary name reachpad) and its three library crates (proto, the frozen
wire protocol; authz, Biscuit verify and offline attenuation; runtime,
the config and tracing shell). Release binaries are built from this source

runners, and every release carries a SHA256SUMS the install script verifies.
To build it yourself (needs Rust and protoc):

Every release tarball also carries a signed build-provenance attestation, so
the chain is checkable without trusting us:

That proves the bytes came out of this repository's release workflow at the
commit the tag names. It rests on no key of ours — the signing identity is a
short-lived credential minted for that one workflow run, and the record is in
a public transparency log.

The snapshot is synced from a private monorepo on every release, so file an
issue rather than a PR for changes; a PR here would be overwritten by the
next sync (the sync script and its header in Cargo.toml say the same).
The CLI is an ordinary client of a public API: it holds no platform secrets
and nothing it does is privileged (the server refuses anything a stranger
could not do).

title: Nine life lessons from the happiest man in the world
description: Stressed out, endlessly scrolling and never satisfied? Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, the Buddhist monk with off-the-charts levels of contentment, may have the answers …
fullText:
Can happiness be taught? I met Mingyur (Rinpoche is an honorary title meaning, roughly, “precious one”) to discover his strategies for a richer life.

“As the Dalai Lama says, we have everything at the touch of a finger, and so when we start to feel lonely, incomplete, bored – we protect ourselves with whatever: eating ice-cream, our smartphone, coffee,” says Mingyur. “We try to get away from them, but those feelings are wisdom, in a way. The really important thing is to sit with them, embrace them as a path to explore.”

For instance, if you find yourself bored while watching a Netflix romcom and simultaneously scrolling on your phone, that’s a signal that ever more stimulation will never be satisfying (science backs this up: one recent study suggests flicking between videos on social media makes us more bored, not less). Take it as a sign to switch everything off, look inward and stop trying to fill the vacuum with superficial stuff.

In 2011, Mingyur left his monastery in the middle of the night with nothing but the clothes on his back, intending to live as a homeless yogi. About three weeks in, he developed severe food poisoning and spent days paralysed by exhaustion and pain – but he now sees this as the moment he started to truly understand the Tibetan Buddhist idea of relinquishing control.

Does he think it’s possible to experience that sort of thing without going through something quite so unpleasant? “Absolutely, of course. Especially nowadays – modern life is full of adventure. When you turn 18, start a new job, start a new relationship – each of those are opportunities for change.” But you don’t have to wait for these bigger moments: meeting a new group of people or taking up a new challenge can help increase your comfort levels with new things. Try implementing one small change every time you feel like you’ve spent a day just going through the motions: a new route home from work, or cooking with one ingredient you’ve never used before. Something I find helpful is to keep a little list of things I want to try whenever I come across them, then when things get stultifying, I’ve got a ready-made buffet to choose from.

“I felt bored the first time I learned meditation,” says Mingyur. “I said, ‘Today is breathing. Tomorrow, again, breathing. The rest of this week, breathing. This is stupid.’ But for meditation, you need to know two things. One, you can make everything support for meditation – you can meditate anytime, anywhere, with anything. Second, you have to have some creative element with your meditation: everything becomes a friend to the meditation.”

To put this another way, if there’s traffic noise outside, or the person next to you is watching TikTok videos, the idea is to let that become a source of focus and calm. This is easier said than done. Mingyur suggests building up to it by listening to music, then waterfalls or birdsong, then loud conversations or construction. Eventually, he says, you should be able to meditate while a baby is crying (I won’t be trying this).

“We think about three things in Tibetan Buddhism: view, meditation and application,” says Mingyur. “View is the mindset: we believe that everybody has an inner sky, the qualities of awareness, love, compassion and wisdom. We practise meditation, and then we practise application – building new habits. So it’s easy to say: ‘Oh, people aren’t nice.’ But of course there are a lot of great qualities in a lot of people, and if you see that, it will manifest. But it’s a habit: you have to keep doing it, and doing it, and then you change.”

Mingyur suggests doing this in a small way every day. Maybe one day try appreciating your family, and the next, find positive things to say about your most annoying colleague.

Yes, gratitude lists can feel a bit peak 2021, but one approach is to go from the incredibly general to the extremely specific. “I appreciate that I have senses, that there’s a roof above me, that I have at least one or two friends or family,” says Mingyur. “When you begin to appreciate these things, you start to appreciate the quality of your life and everything around you.”

This doesn’t necessarily mean you need to start a gratitude journal. After a few days, it can feel a bit too easy for your mind to scribble another ‘I’m grateful for my children’. Instead, the idea is to use little moments of downtime to notice how nice it is to be in the specific moment, whether you’re sitting in a comfortable chair or watching your child swing a stick around in the woods.

“I had panic attacks when I was young,” says Mingyur. “When I began to learn meditation from my father, I asked him how to fight them. He said: ‘Don’t fight.’ The first reason is that if you fight, panic becomes stronger. It’s like saying: ‘Don’t think about orange’ – suddenly it’s all you can think about.

And the second thing my father said is, there’s no need to push panic away, because it’s like a storm cloud in the sky. A storm cloud can’t change the nature of the sky – it comes and then it goes. You just have to connect with the inner sky.” To put this another way, whatever inner turmoil you’re going through, remind yourself that it isn’t actually changing anything fundamental in your brain: it will pass and things will feel better.

At times of extreme distress, this might feel impossible. In which case, Mingyur suggests we focus on physical sensations – the temperature of the room, the sounds around you – to help deal with the panic in that moment, rather than trying to tell ourselves everything is fine.

“Genuine happiness is when we let go of that feeling of dissatisfaction, incompleteness, that something is missing,” says Mingyur. “But if you only look for happiness, then you will get the opposite. People often think, ‘I’ll be happy if I make more money, or if I move to this new country or get this new job or win the lottery’ – but that just changes your happiness a little bit and then you go back to baseline, right? But if you practise breathing, love and compassion, you can move that baseline over time.”

To start, simply sit and breathe naturally, focusing on the rise and fall of your abdomen or the sensation of the air passing through your body. As you’re doing this, you might try mentally repeating a simple mantra (“May I be happy and free from suffering” is a common one) to cultivate love towards yourself, and then extending that compassion to loved ones, pets and, eventually, all the other people in your life.

“What we call awareness is like sunlight, and our emotional patterns are like frost on the grass in the morning,” says Mingyur. “When the sunlight manifests, the frost melts automatically – there’s no fight. I talk to some business leaders who are really stressed. They have to do so many things at the same time, so they build the habit of being stressed or angry all the time. They come to me and say: ‘My relationship is not good,’ or ‘There’s a problem between me and the boss.’ I say, ‘Just catch the anger. Be with the anger. Just for a second.’ Once you catch it, you have a choice, it can transform.”

To put this another way, when you’re momentarily furious at someone – at work or at home – you don’t need to meditate for 10 minutes; just avoid your autopilot response of snapping at them by noticing the fact that you’re angry, and then watching as the emotion melts away. From experience, I can say that this takes practice – but it’s definitely worth working on.

“If you can really help others, you feel a different level of happiness from having an ice-cream or a coffee,” says Mingyur. We all know this, obviously – but how often are we actually doing it? Check in on a neighbour in need today.

title: Microsoft's Maia 200 AI Accelerator at Hot Chips 2026
description: At Hot Chips 2026, Microsoft is going into new detail on Maia 200, their second-generation server AI inference processor
fullText:
The fourth AI accelerator presentation of Hot Chips 2026 comes from Microsoft, who like so many other hyperscalers has gone into the business of designing their own AI accelerator. Now in their second generation, Microsoft is preparing to deploy their Maia 200 accelerator inside their Azure data centers. The 3nm chip was announced early this year, while today’s presentation will be the deepest Microsoft has gone into the chip’s architecture and the many design tweaks they have made to improve its performance over the original Maia 100.

This article is being written live from the presentation, so please excuse any typos.

Maia is notable right off the bat for not being quite as aggressive of a design in terms of chip size. Though by no means a small chip at 140 billion transistors, Microsoft has paired the accelerator with just 6 stacks of HBM3e memory, and the total chip TDP is just 750 Watts. Though as these are designed to go into racks (just as with any other AI accelerator), the performance and power consumption still add up quickly.

Today is going to the story of how Microsoft designed the Maia 200. The talk will go over the goals of the architecture, the SoC and its architecture, and how it comes together to form the larger system, with software layered in on top.

Inference has a very diverse workload between prefill and decode. Mixture of expert modeling also creates a diversity of workloads. These and more were the design target of the Maia 200.

Maia 200 uses the Software Defined Local Acces (SLDA) dataflow architecture. Microsoft makes a distinction of architecture along two dimensions: data access and data movement. SDLA is defined by the fact that the dataflow is software-defined, while data access is completely local. This organization is similar to the Flynn’s classic taxonomy of processors.

The SDLA architecture affords a high degree of determinism. The dataflow is controlled in software, and thus is set at compile time which means it is known is advance. Meanwhile Microsoft is able to avoid a lot of cross-talk and heavy bandwidth/fabric needs by keeping data access within the compute elements.

Here is an abstract look at the control and data path flow of the architecture. DMA and processing elements run the data path; each one has its own hardware queue of instructions. Explicit sync is achieved via semaphores.

Control, I/O, and compute are all running independently, and being chained/synced via the aforementioned semaphores.

Microsoft’s fundamental computing block is a tile. Each tile contains a tile tensor unit (TTU) their matrix math engine, the tile vector processor (TVP) with SIMD engines, and then the tile control processor (TCP). Rounding out th etile is a TDMA block, and then an L1 cache block.

Microsoft employs a hierarchical memory structure, with L1 (tiler) and L2 (cluster) cache layers below the memory layer. Data is only moved between layers when it is needed to do so.

As for I/O, Microsoft uses a custom NIC and interconnect protocol as their network fabric. Reliability is a first-class design parameter here, with hardware-based recovery mechanisms. This custom design is achieved with minimal die space on Maia 200.

Each SoC has 8 Ethernet lanes, split up into four network planes.

Maia 200 also heavily emphasizes load balancing both inside a chip and across all of the chips in a cluster. Effective load balancing is fundamental to allowing Maia 200 to scale up to large domains.

Maia 200 is built on TSMC 3nm, with a 750 Watt TDP. There is 7TB/second of HBM bandwidth, accomplished via 6 HBM stacks. In terms of compute throughput, the chip offers 10,000 TFLOPS of FP4 performance. The SoC die is 820mm2 altogether.

Microsoft uses a fully connected quad topology for their networking.

There is no scale-out networking for Maia 200. It is all scale-up networking. Microsoft’s slide demonstrates 128 racks with 6000 chips all together. Microsoft took a bet on unified Ethernet here, and it has paid off with operational simplicity. Each rack has tier-0 switches to connect the nodes within the racks, and then tier-1 switches to connect the racks themselves.

Shifting over to the software side of Microsoft’s ecosystem, they didn’t just co-design the chip and system, but they co-designed the entire stack right on through the software. The software at the core of this is the Microsoft Collective Communication Library (MCCL).

The SDLA design of the hardware requires that the kernels running on the hardware be tuned for the hardware for the best performance.

GEMM workloads are one of the fundamental workloads run on Maia 200. Above, Microsoft’s presentation lays out how a batch GEMM workload is handled on the chip. A gather operation takes place over the central GNOC, while the weights are loaded from HBM, and finally the output is pinned to the L1 SRAM.

Of course, Maia 200 chips aren’t meant to be used alone; they are meant to be used together in a scale-up domain. So here is a look at the distributed workflow for batch GEMMs.

Data reuse is also a very important element of execution on Maia 200 for efficiency purposes, as it reduces the memory traffic flowing across the trip. Block interleaving is used to get fully overlapped tensor/SIMD operations.

Microsoft uses an adaptive logical topology for collectives. A collective can complete with a single hop and no overhead.

Maia also supports a ring-based topology for when large transfers are needed.

Now here is a look at the performance of the Maia 200 in GEMM benchmarks. Points on the left are memory-bound, points on the right are compute-bound. Maia gets very close to its theoretical maximum (roofline) in these benchmarks.

Meanwhile attention benchmarks show an effective peak of 1.65 PFLOPS.

Finally, here is a look at collective benchmarking. Microsoft is able to reach almost 1.3TB/second in BF16 AllReduce (with the chart also showing how the different broadcast implementations affect performance), while All2All peaks at 655 GB/second.

And that is a quick look at Maia 200. Microsoft has opted for a data-movement-centric architecture with SDLA, and paired this with a unified all-Ethernet networking structure to keep the networking simple. Software is the third pillar of Maia 200, with the classical software development house co-designing the hardware and software in concert to optimize the very explicit flow of data.

title: Utilities Break California Lobbying Record Under Newsom While Former Aides Lead
description: New disclosures show utilities spent a record $16.7 million lobbying Sacramento through the first six quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session as…
fullText:
New disclosures show utilities spent a record $16.7 million lobbying Sacramento through the first six quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session as lawmakers consider a utility bailout in end of session scramble

Sacramento, CA— California’s three largest investor-owned utilities — Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E), Southern California Edison (Edison), and Sempra Energy (Sempra) — have already mounted the most expensive lobbying campaign in state history, spending $16.7 million lobbying Governor Gavin Newsom’s administration, the Legislature and state regulators through the first six reporting quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session, according to new disclosures released today.

Consumer Watchdog’s review of CAL-ACCESS lobbying records dating back to the 1999–2000 legislative sessionfound the current session has already surpassed every previous utility lobbying campaign on record — even though two quarterly reporting periods remain before the session concludes.

At the same time, utilities have increasingly declined to answer reporters’ questions directly, instead referring media inquiries to Wildfire Victims First, a new disinformation coalition funded entirely by California’s investor-owned utilities and utility political committees. Despite its name, the organization is not funded by independent wildfire survivor groups but instead is pushing a utility bailout in an end of session scramble. The coalition’s spokesman, Nathan Click, previously served as Governor Gavin Newsom’s communications director and chief spokesman before founding the Sacramento communications firm now representing the organization. Consumer Watchdog also found that Wildfire Victims First’s television advertising is being placed by Polaris Campaign Media, the affiliated media-buying firm of Bearstar Strategies, Governor Newsom’s longtime political consulting firm.

Utilities spent more than $4.35 million lobbying Sacramento during the second quarter of 2026 alone, including more than $353,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission. PG&E accounted for nearly three-quarters of all utility lobbying reported during the quarter, spending nearly $3.2 million.

Through the first six reporting quarters of the 2025–2026 legislative session, PG&E, Edison and Sempra have spent a combined $16.7 million lobbying state government, including $15.9 million on general lobbying and more than $870,000 lobbying the California Public Utilities Commission.

Consumer Watchdog’s review of lobbying disclosures since Governor Gavin Newsom took office shows utility lobbying has climbed dramatically during his administration. The previous high-water mark came during the 2023–2024 legislative session, when utilities spent $16.1 million lobbying Sacramento. With two quarterly reporting periods still remaining, the 2025–2026 session has already surpassed that total, making it the most expensive utility lobbying campaign and under the Newsom administration.

The record-breaking lobbying campaign comes during one of the most consequential legislative sessions for California’s investor-owned utilities in years, as lawmakers and regulators decide who ultimately pays the costs of catastrophic wildfires:

“Utilities aren’t just spending record amounts lobbying Sacramento,” said Carmen Balber, Executive Director of Consumer Watchdog. “This is the largest utility lobbying campaign in modern California history, unfolding as Governor Newsom considers another end-of-session utility bailout. While utilities marshal lobbyists, political consultants and public relations campaigns, wildfire survivors are fighting to preserve their legal rights. That’s the worst of California politics.”

“They burned down our homes. Now they’re spending millions pretending to be wildfire survivors while real survivors fight to get home. Together with millions of Americans, we call on Governor Newsom to stop bailing out utility monopolies and start protecting the people they harmed,” said Joy Chen, founder of Every Fire Survivor’s Network.

Every Fire Survivor’s Network and Consumer Watchdog are leading the No Utility Bailouts campaign at DearNewsom.org, a coalition of public officials and organizations representing more than 3.5 million Americansurging Governor Newsom to reject another utility bailout.

The dual lobbying and communications strategy reflect the extraordinary political stakes surrounding California’s wildfire and insurance crisis, where Governor Newsom has emerged as the central decision-maker. With a new legislative bailout language expected this month, the outcome of those debates could determine who ultimately bears the cost of California’s next catastrophic wildfire — utility shareholders, taxpayers, ratepayers or survivors themselves.

“When utilities are simultaneously mounting the most expensive lobbying campaign in California history while Governor Newsom’s former chief spokesman serves as the face of their utility-funded coalition and his longtime political consulting network helps promote its message, Californians have every reason to ask whether utility influence has become too deeply embedded in the state’s decision-making. Wildfire survivors deserve transparency, accountability and confidence that these decisions are being made in the public interest, not the utilities’.”
