title: Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor as impasse with US drags on
description: Iran said it had restarted talks with neighbor Oman to manage the Strait of Hormuz as it faces heightened economic pressure from U. President Donald Trump in the ‌wider confl...
fullText:
CAIRO, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Iran said it had restarted talks with neighbor Oman to manage the Strait of Hormuz as it faces heightened economic pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump in the ‌wider conflict.

Iran and Oman have been in on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic ‌waterway, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February.

Most shipping has been shut down since then.

The ​two countries said on Tuesday that they discussed "a joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines.

Trump said all mines in the strait had been cleared, repeating comments that he has previously made.

Though active hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have largely subsided, diplomatic efforts to reach a peace deal have stalled and passage through the waterway ‌remains perilous.

An oil tanker was struck on Tuesday ⁠by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 nautical miles (17 km) northeast of Oman's Ash Shishah, which lies at the entrance to the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said.

Separately, ⁠the U.S. Secret Service said on Tuesday that it was aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate Trump's youngest son, Barron.

A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state TV discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron ​Trump, 20, ​claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a $10 ​million bounty had been offered for his killing.

Despite ‌the ongoing tensions, the U.S. is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity.

In an effort to hobble Iran's economy, the United States earlier this week threatened to punish countries that continue to ‌do business with Iran, but said it would not impose penalties ​immediately.

Oil prices fell for a second day as traders brushed off the ​impact of the U.S. sanctions, while Iran denounced the ​U.S. effort to isolate its economy as an act of "gross lawlessness", expressing confidence that many ‌countries would not join the pressure campaign.

U.S. public approval ​of the war has fallen ​to its lowest level since the conflict's early days, and Trump's popularity is likewise at a record low ahead of congressional elections in November, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.

Thousands of people have died in the conflict, most ​of them in Iran and Lebanon, while ‌the U.S. and Israel have degraded much of Iran's conventional military capacity. The exact state of its ​nuclear program, which the U.S. and Israel aim to dismantle, remains unknown.

(Additional reporting by Reuters bureaux; Writing ​by Costas Pitas; Editing by Andy Sullivan and Sanjeev Miglani)

title: Tropical Storm Julio dissipates near Tropical Storm Iselle in the Pacific Ocean
description: Tropical Storm Julio in the Pacific Ocean was on track Tuesday to be absorbed by the stronger Tropical Storm Iselle, which is churning to the north.  The National Hurricane Center based in Miami annou...
fullText:
MIAMI (AP) — Tropical Storm Julio in the Pacific Ocean was on track Tuesday to be absorbed by the stronger Tropical Storm Iselle, which is churning to the north.

The National Hurricane Center based in Miami announced early Tuesday morning that Julio had formed. It was centered about 630 miles (1,010 kilometers) west of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico. Julio had maximum sustained winds of about 45 mph (75 kph).

Forecasters said Julio would be absorbed by Iselle later Tuesday. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect for either storm.

Iselle was about 775 miles (1,245 kilometers) west of the Baja California peninsula and had winds of 60 mph (95 kph).

In the Central Pacific, Tropical Storm Lala continued to churn with 50 mph (80 kph) winds but wasn't threatening land. Earlier this month as a hurricane, the outer bands of Lala battered Hawaii and caused destructive flooding.

And Moke was no longer considered a tropical cyclone after skirting Hawaii as a tropical storm, the center said.

title: Trump criticism leads to rare criminal charges for Air Force officer who called for impeachment
description: A US airman who was arrested twice, once on the steps of the US Capitol while calling for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, was officially criminally charged Monday for his comments, accordin...
fullText:
A US airman who was arrested twice, once on the steps of the US Capitol while calling for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, was officially criminally charged Monday for his comments, according to a charging document his attorney shared with CNN.

Maj. Jason Watson faces the following charges under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, according to the document: three violations of Article 88 for alleged "contemptuous" remarks about Trump, five violations of Article 92 for allegedly disobeying orders and two violations of Article 133 for alleged conduct unbecoming an officer.

An Air Force spokesperson confirmed the charges on Tuesday.

"Maj. Watson will continue to be held in pre-trial confinement," the spokesperson said. "Airmen are afforded the right to due process, and considered innocent until proven guilty, in accordance with the Uniform Code of Military Justice."

The rare Article 88 charges are connected to the Air Force officer's June interview with the Defenders of our Republic Substack newsletter, his July 1 protest in uniform at the US Capitol, and an August 17 CNN interview.

It can be considered a violation of the Uniform Code of Military Justice to participate in uniform in any overtly partisan activity, such as a political protest, or to use "contemptuous words" against the president and other high-ranking civilian officials. Many low-level offenses of these rules are resolved informally, but Watson's violations were unusually high-profile.

Watson was first arrested in July while protesting in uniform at the US Capitol, and he was then arrested again last week just days after criticizing Trump again during a CNN interview. One of his attorneys, Chris Mutimer, told CNN that his client was ordered to remain in "pre-trial confinement" — an action analogous to a denial of bond in civilian court — pending legal action against him.

"Not only is (Trump) a failure as president, he is flagrantly violating the Constitution, breaking the law, engaged in rampant corruption, and is killing Americans," Watson told CNN's Erin Burnett during the interview. "And that is unacceptable to me."

In July, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said in a social media post that he expected all airmen to "comply with all laws and policies government personal conduct, political participation, and the wear of the uniform."

"Americans place their trust in us," Meink said. "We cannot, and will not, compromise the trust of the nation."

The disobeying orders charges against Watson allege that he violated Defense Department regulations barring troops from speaking out in favor of partisan causes; "wrongfully" wore his uniform at a Capitol press conference; broke leave regulations by traveling to Washington, DC; and refused to wear his uniform to work the morning after his CNN interview.

Air Force prosecutors also alleged that Watson's Capitol protest and CNN interview constituted "conduct unbecoming an officer."

Mutimer, Watson's attorney, told CNN's Erin Burnett on "OutFront" that he spoke with his client Monday and "he is basically in solitary confinement for his safety."

Mutimer said, "He truly believes in everything about our constitution and what it represents, and the oath that he swore, and he stands by the fact that he did this so others wouldn't have to, and to share that to anyone who's scared and feels alone."

The founder of the organization that organized the protest in July, Jessica Denson of the Removal Coalition, told CNN at the time that Watson was aware of the risks of what he was doing and had reached out to them via email.

"We started having conversations and took this desire that he had to come out very seriously and thought about the best way to make his sacrifice worth it," Denson said.

Military courts-martial leading to "contempt of officials" charges are rare — a CNN review only identified two such convictions that have occurred since the modern Uniform Code of Military Justice was enacted in 1951.

In 1965, an Army lieutenant was convicted of the charge after he participated in an off-base protest against the Vietnam War in El Paso, Texas. Lt. Henry Howe was sentenced to a dismissal from the service — the equivalent of a dishonorable discharge for an officer — and a year in the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Defense Secretary Robert McNamara ultimately granted parole to Howe, ending his sentence early.

The most recent Article 88 conviction came in 2021, when former Marine Corps Lt. Col. Stuart Scheller pleaded guilty to contempt of officials and other charges linked to a series of social media videos he published criticizing the Biden administration's handling of the US military's withdrawal from Afghanistan. Scheller, who was confined to the brig for a period of time before his trial, was sentenced to a $5,000 pay forfeiture and resigned from the Marine Corps sans-pension as part of a plea agreement.

The Trump administration has since appointed Scheller to serve as a senior adviser to the Pentagon's undersecretary for personnel and readiness.

Frank Rosenblatt, a retired Army judge advocate and associate law professor at Mississippi Christian University, said to CNN that the standard for "contemptuous" words is "less than precise" in guidance provided to military judges and panel members (similar to jurors).

Rosenblatt said that "contemptuous" remarks under Article 88 must be "insulting, rude, and disdainful conduct, or otherwise disrespectfully attributing to another a quality of meanness, disreputableness, or worthlessness."

He suggested that a pretrial hearing known as an Article 32 proceeding may be required to assess whether Watson's remarks instead "are true or are fair criticisms" of the president.

It remains to be seen whether Watson's case will be referred to trial, and whether that trial will be considered a special or general court-martial. Special courts-martial are roughly equivalent to misdemeanor trials, and general courts-martial are analogous to felony trials and can hand down more severe sentences.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN's Piper Hudspeth Blackburn, Carmen Conte Widman and Francesca Giuliani Hoffman contributed to this report.

Davis Winkie's work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

title: Are left-handers better and when will Root catch Tendulkar? Cricket Q&A
description: Data analysts CricViz answer your questions on successful reviews, hat-tricks, Joe Root and more.
fullText:
During England's first Test against Pakistan, we asked BBC Sport readers to send statistical questions for our colleagues at CricViz.

Our new feature, Ask CricViz, is here to help and we can reveal the first selection of answers below.

Please note that all stats in Tests are inclusive of the recent Australia v Bangladesh Test in Mackay, but do not include stats from the ongoing Sri Lanka v India Test in Colombo.

Graham, Hastings: Against Pakistan, Josh Tongue took two wickets in two balls but missed out on his hat-trick. What is the 'conversion rate' from having two in two, to going on and getting the hat-trick?

CricViz: In Tests where such data is available in our database, there have been 1,355 occasions where a bowler has taken wickets in two consecutive balls, with only 43 (3.2%) of them converted to a hat-trick.

There have been a total of 49 hat-tricks in Test history but we have the ball-by-ball details for 43 of them.

Across his Test career, Josh Tongue has had two wickets in two balls on four occasions and yet no hat-tricks. The four instances include the two occasions in the last Test versus Pakistan at Headingley, once in the Ashes Test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in December 2025, and against India at Headingley in June 2025.

Here's another interesting bit: Australia's Mitchell Starc has taken wickets in two consecutive balls on 17 occasions in Tests but is yet to register a hat-trick.

Charles Dennett, Lichfield: When Joe Root was involved in a 50-run partnership with Jordan Cox, it made me think that he must be close to being the player involved in the most 50-run partnerships with the greatest number of distinct batting partners. Is this true?

CricViz: You're spot on with your observation. In the partnership of 150 with Jordan Cox at Headingley, Joe Root has now registered 50-plus run partnerships with 45 distinct partners in Test, the joint-most - tied with Shivnarine Chanderpaul from West Indies.

Also interestingly, that partnership with Jordan Cox was the 88th time Joe Root has been involved in a 100-plus partnership, the joint-most in Test history on par with Rahul Dravid from India.

Harvey, Dartford: After hearing about Ollie Robinson's terrific stats with balls bowled hitting the stumps, can you tell us the bowler (seamer or spinner) who has the highest percentage of their balls bowled that would go on to hit the stumps?

CricViz: In the ball-tracking era (since 2006) former Pakistan all-rounder Mohammad Hafeez has the highest percentage of balls projected to hit the stumps at 41%. When considering only pace bowlers, Paul Collingwood leads the way with just under 19% of his deliveries hitting the stumps.

Tests in Bangladesh have the highest percentage of deliveries hitting the stumps at 27%, no surprise considering the amount of spin bowled. The fast and bouncy pitches of Australia have historically seen just 12% of deliveries hit the stumps, however, the lowest for any nation.

Ben, Llangrannog: Which batter has had the greatest success with decision review system (DRS) reviews?

CricViz: Of the 35 batters to have taken 15 or more reviews in all Tests since the start of 2016, Bangladesh's Liton Das has the highest success rate with 68.8% (11 out of 16) of his DRS reviews overturned by the umpire, followed by India's Cheteshwar Pujara with 60% (9 out of 15) and West Indies' Kraigg Brathwaite with 55.6% (10 out of 18).

If you look at this from a bowler's perspective, of the 58 bowlers to have taken 15 or more reviews in all Tests since the start of 2016, West Indies' Kemar Roach has the highest success rate with 35% (14 out of 40) of his DRS reviews overturned by the umpire, followed by England's Chris Woakes with 29.4% (10 out of 34) and Stuart Broad with 29.1% (16 out of 55).

Jack, Tanzania: If he continues at his current rate, when is Joe Root predicted to beat Tendulkar's run record in Test matches?

CricViz: Joe Root is currently on 14,180 Test runs, 1,741 runs behind Sachin Tendulkar's tally of 15,921. In Tests since the start of 2024, Root has scored 2,794 runs in 32 Tests and 58 innings, scoring 47.6 runs per innings on average. If he continues scoring at the same rate, he will need another 37 innings to go past Tendulkar's run record. That could approximately be around 20 Tests.

As of now, until the end of the next home summer in England, Root has another 14 Tests to go, with two more Tests left in this current series against Pakistan, three away Tests in South Africa in December and January 2027, two away Tests in Bangladesh in February 2027, a one-off 150th Anniversary Test match versus Australia at the MCG in March 2027, followed by one home Test versus Bangladesh at Lord's in May 2027, and the five Ashes Tests in June and August 2027.

It could be 15 Tests until the end of the next summer if England convert their slim chance to qualify for the final of the World Test Championship (WTC).

Current World Test Championship standings

Freddie Davidson, Northampton: Who has the highest average across all formats over the last 10 years, all-format player?

CricViz: Since the start of 2016 in men's internationals, 43 players have scored at least 1,500 runs in men's Tests, 1,000 runs in ODIs and 500 runs in T20Is.

Of these 43 players, Virat Kohli's average of 56.4 is the highest in these last 10 years. Kohli averages 48.3 in Tests, 67.6 in ODIs and 50.3 in T20Is.

Joe Belham, Manchester: Is there any data to prove if left-handed or right-handed batters are better across the history of the sport? Commentators often suggest that left-handed batters are more attractive on the eye and I've always thought that must be nonsense!

CricViz: Looking at this in terms of batting average, in all three international formats in both the men's and women's formats, left-handed batters fare better compared to right-handed batters (if we're looking at just the recognised batters playing in the top seven in the batting order).

Ben Snowball, Surrey: At what specific pace (mph) has there been the most wickets in Test cricket for fast bowlers?

CricViz: In Tests where ball-tracking data is available (since the start of 2006), if we break down all wickets in a 1mph range, deliveries from pace bowlers in the 84-85mph range have seen the most wickets with 1,594 in total. If you break the speeds down to a single decimal, 84.6 mph has been the most productive wicket-taking delivery with 193 wickets in total.

Leo, London: In the wake of Bazball, I would love to see breakdowns of risk/reward for various players and various shots. In general, do you have statistics on outcomes for forward defensives, cuts, drives, hooks, pulls, etc?

CricViz: Looking at the last three years of shot type data against pace in Test cricket, the dismissal rate for some 'attacking' shots is relatively similar to that of defensive strokes, with defensive shots seeing a dismissal every 41 deliveries, similar to that of cut shots (40.4 balls per dismissal) and flicks (38.1 balls per dismissal).

While batters may be striking at 123 when driving, their dismissal rate sits at 31.9, 10 balls lower than that of defensive strokes. Hook (15 balls per dismissal) and pull (22.7 balls per dismissal) shots hover around the 150 mark in terms of strike-rate but with a much more frequent dismissal rate compared to defending.

Batters are dismissed every 295.5 balls when leaving; a good leave is certainly the best shot in the book when it comes to keeping your wicket intact.

Chris Crighton, Stanmore: What ball of the over takes the most wickets? My money is on the sixth!

CricViz: Well, unfortunately it's not the sixth ball, Chris. In Test cricket, the second ball of the over has seen the most wickets fall on 11,866 occasions, followed by the fifth ball with 11,787 wickets. This takes into account Tests with such ball-by-ball data where we've had four balls, five balls and eight balls in an over and now finally settling to the standard six.

Chris, Derbyshire: What is the most common score in Test match cricket (team and individual)?

CricViz: Most common team score in Tests: 296 (44 instances), followed by 191 (43 instances) and then 223 (42 instances).

Most common individual score in Tests: As expected, 0 with 11,877 instances followed by 1 (4,684 instances) and then 4 (3,897 instances). Note that the score of 0 here includes all instances of a batter coming to bat including dismissals and not outs.

Ben, Natland: How many times did Mahendra Singh Dhoni hit a six to win a game? And is he the person to do this the most times?

CricViz: MS Dhoni has hit a six to win an ODI or T20I on 12 occasions, the most by any batter in limited-overs in international cricket.

Most instances to win a game with a six in run-chases in ODIs and T20Is:

MS Dhoni - 12 (ODIs - 9, T20Is - 3)

Virat Kohli - 9 (ODIs - 5, T20Is - 4)

Eoin Morgan - 8 (ODIs - 3, T20Is - 5)

Jos Buttler - 8 (ODIs - 5, T20Is - 3)

Shoaib Malik - 7 (ODIs - 4, T20Is - 3)

KL Rahul - 7 (ODIs - 6, T20Is - 1)

Can you name the top 20 Test batters in the world?

Can you name world's top 20 men's Test bowlers?

title: Leeds and Rangers co-owner jailed after prostitution arrest
description: Jed York pleaded no contest to two charges in Ohio after being arrested for soliciting prostitution.
fullText:
Leeds and Rangers co-owner Jed York has been jailed in Ohio after being arrested for soliciting prostitution.

The 45-year-old, who is also the owner of the San Francisco 49ers, was convicted of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools after pleading no contest to two charges.

In the Ohio legal system, a no contest plea means a defendant accepts a conviction without formally admitting guilt.

York was sentenced to one day in jail on each offence, to be served concurrently, and was given credit for time already served.

York was fined $150 for disorderly conduct and $1,000 for possessing criminal tools.

Court records show the case was brought by East Palestine Police Department and filed at Columbiana County Municipal Court on Monday.

York pleaded no contest to both charges at an arraignment hearing and was found guilty.

Court records also show an expungement request was filed and denied on the same day. This is a request to have records destroyed or sealed so they are not accessible to the public.

According to reports in the US media, other court documents say York responded to an advertisement on a prostitution website placed by undercover officers from a Human Trafficking Task Force in Ohio.

These documents say he arranged to have sexual activity with a woman in exchange for $140 (£103).

In a plea deal, the original charge was reduced to disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools - thought to refer to the phone used to reply to the advert.

The 49ers were part of the US consortium who took control of Rangers last year but York is not involved in the day-to-day running of the club.

Rangers and Leeds have both said they will not be commenting.

The 49ers said: "As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time."

York became a co-owner of Rangers through 49ers Enterprises, the investment arm linked to the NFL's San Francisco 49ers, where he serves as chief executive and principal owner.

In May 2025, a consortium led by US businessman Andrew Cavenagh and 49ers Enterprises completed a takeover of Rangers after acquiring a controlling 51% stake in the Scottish Premiership club.

Cavenagh became Rangers chairman, with 49ers Enterprises taking a leading role in the club's ownership.

The takeover followed months of negotiations and brought Rangers under majority American-backed ownership.

49ers Enterprises first invested in Leeds United in 2018 when the club was in the Championship, steadily increasing its investment as the Whites returned to the Premier League following a 16-year absence, before assuming full control in 2023.

As an NFL owner, York is subject to league policies. "We are aware of the matter which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy," the NFL said.

title: St Helens legend Lomax to retire at end of season
description: St Helens legend Jonny Lomax announces he is to retire at the end of the Super League season.
fullText:
St Helens legend Jonny Lomax has announced he is to retire at the end of the Super League season.

The 35-year-old, who has not featured since fracturing his jaw in the defeat by Warrington Wolves in June, has made 388 appearances for Saints, winning five Grand Finals, one Challenge Cup and a World Club Challenge.

He won four caps for Great Britain and 11 for England, including a World Cup final appearance against Australia in 2017.

"Over the last 20 years, I have been able to live out a boyhood dream. Achieving far more than I could ever have imagined. Representing and captaining my hometown club and, of course, the pinnacle, representing England and Great Britain," he told the club website., external

"I have been fortunate enough to meet some incredible people along the way, experiencing some incredible highs with them. As well as some testing times too."

He added: "I will retire at the age of 36, grateful for the life the game has given me, knowing I have given it everything I could, with the scars to prove it (19 operations, including 12 knee operations by the age of 26). Despite this, I still feel lucky.

"For those that have supported me throughout it all… I hope I have been able to do you proud."

Saints chairman Eamonn McManus called Lomax, who made his debut in March 2009 aged 18, "the bravest of brave in the bravest of sports".

St Helens are seventh in Super League with three games of the campaign to go.

They are two points behind reigning champions Hull KR, who they play in the final game of the regular season, as they look to secure a place in the top six and avoid missing out on the Super League play-offs for the first time.

title: LIV returnees should 'eat humble pie' - Faldo
description: Sir Nick Faldo says LIV golfers seeking a return to the DP World Tour may have to "eat a bit of humble pie" before regaining eligibility for the European-based circuit.
fullText:
Sir Nick Faldo says LIV golfers seeking a return to the DP World Tour may have to "eat a bit of humble pie" before regaining eligibility for the European-based circuit.

LIV's 2026 season ended last Sunday in Indianapolis after this week's cancellation of the breakaway tour's Team Championship in Michigan.

Tyrrell Hatton, Tom McKibbin and Adrian Meronk are competing instead at the Husqvarna British Masters starting on Thursday.

Six-time major champion Faldo is promoting the Belfry tournament while LIV's boss Scott O'Neil continues his quest to replace Saudi Arabian funding. He wants $350m (£258m) investment to keep the league operating next year.

"I'm hearing there are more players wanting to leave LIV than want to stay," Faldo told BBC Sport.

"So it doesn't sound good for them for the future."

Hatton, McKibbin and Meronk are able to compete as DP World Tour members after accepting a deal that allowed them to play both tours without sanction this year.

For his walk on music at the Indianapolis tournament last week, Hatton chose Queen's I Want to Break Free, interpreted as a firm signal that the Englishman wants to leave the tour that began in 2022.

Hatton has recent tournament wins that protect his DP World status. Two-time major champion Jon Rahm also has exemptions that would qualify him for the tour should he quit the previously Saudi Arabia-funded outfit.

But Faldo is clear that it should not be overly easy for LIV players to walk straight back onto the DP World Tour.

"How do they actually give them a route back?" Faldo added.

"You know, given the way they've disrupted - go and start again. Go back to tour school.

"Hey, you might have to eat a bit of humble pie and say, well, I want to be a proper golfer again, and so I've got to start back where I'm meant to be and I'll work my way up the good old way with my skills and my scoring."

'Tough road back' to PGA Tour from LIV - McIlroy

DeChambeau proud of what LIV has achieved

How potential returnees are to be treated was high on the agenda when the DP World Tour's tournament committee met on Tuesday afternoon.

PGA chief executive officer Brian Rolapp said there are no "current plans" to offer LIV players a route back.

"I don't know the future of LIV," he added.

"We've been consistent. Anyone who's interested in coming to the PGA Tour needs to demonstrate that they are relieved of their contractual commitments or any tail obligations they might have in that legacy model."

While America's PGA Tour imposed blanket one-year bans on members who competed on the LIV tour, their European counterparts take a more nuanced approach.

With many leading Europeans based in the United States, the Wentworth-based organisation would like as many big names as it can get.

At the same time they have to protect the rest of the membership who remained loyal to the tour.

"It is a difficult jigsaw to piece together and we have to work out how to treat these players should they want to leave LIV and rejoin," said a senior tour source.

Faldo said: "We can negotiate. If a player has some form of exemption on the tour already, someone like Rahm would obviously carry it through majors and that sort of thing.

"But all the other guys, you know, they did cause quite a disruption in the world of golf. You know, they were in a way invited into LIV. And that's not how golf is, is it?

"We all had to do the good old Monday qualifying back in the day, 50 blooming years ago. I personally think that's the way it should be, you start again and climb the ladder."

Chile's Joaquin Niemann was one of the most successful players on the LIV tour, amassing more than £60m in prize money. But the 27-year-old is currently ineligible for both the PGA and DP World Tours.

Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter and Sergio Garcia - all distinguished Ryder Cup players for Europe - are others whose status could be up for debate.

Exciting young Spaniard Josele Ballester and American Peter Uihlein are LIV golfers who have entered the first stage of DP World Tour qualifying school at Huddersfield on 2 September.

title: Vondrousova appeals to Cas against four-year ban
description: Former Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova did not let an anti-doping official enter her home to carry out a test in December 2025 and her ban is set to run until June 2030.
fullText:
Former Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova has appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) against her four-year ban for refusing an anti-doping test.

The 27-year-old was handed the ban in June after the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) charged her with denying a doping control officer entry to her home to conduct an out-of-competition test in December 2025.

Her suspension is due to end on 21 June 2030.

Cas confirmed to BBC Sport that it had received the appeal but said a hearing date had not yet been set.

Vondrousova, who in 2023 became the first unseeded player to win the Wimbledon women's singles title, said in April that when she refused the test she was at "breaking point after months of physical and mental stress".

The Czech added that she feared for her safety when the officer called at her home at 20:00 on 3 December and said they failed to properly identify themselves or follow "protocol". She signed a refusal form when she went outside to walk her dog shortly afterwards.

However, a tribunal determined Vondrousova provided "no compelling justification" for refusing the test, nor to receive a shortened ban.

Mental stress led to anti-doping charge - Vondrousova

Dog walk and expletive text - key findings in Vondrousova anti-doping case

Players are required to log their whereabouts for an allotted hour each day so authorities can conduct anti-doping tests outside of competition.

Vondrousova, a former French Open finalist and Olympic silver medallist, wrote in a statement following her ban: "I have never doped, I have never had a positive test. Throughout my entire career I have undergone countless anti-doping controls and have always stepped on the court with a clear conscience."

The former world number six hasn't played since reaching the second round of the Adelaide International in January and has slipped down to 153rd in the WTA rankings.

title: What does your Premier League club still need in the transfer window?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at what each of the Premier League clubs still need before the summer transfer window shuts in seven days.
fullText:
The first weekend of the Premier League season is complete but clubs still have one week of the transfer window remaining to secure last-minute squad additions.

Results are one thing but for many managers and sporting directors their opening match was an eye-opener in what positions need to be strengthened, who is no longer needed and what gaps still need to be plugged.

With the transfer window closing on Tuesday, 1 September at 23:00 BST, BBC Sport takes a look at what each top-flight club still needs and fans also have their say.

The Premier League champions have already strengthened the middle of the pitch with Bruno Guimaraes, the wing with Christos Tzolis and their defence with Ezri Konsa.

But Arsenal are still in the market for a forward and have a long-standing interest in Julian Alvarez.

Although it appears to be a difficult deal due to many factors, the Gunners will be ready to act if there is a chance to get it done.

If you want someone who is Premier League proven, who has won it all from the World Cup to the Champions League, Julian Alvarez looks like the guy that can take Arsenal to the promised land of finally getting over the line in Europe. Especially when there aren't that many elite forwards in the world.

Alvarez's Arsenal dilemma amid summer's most bitter transfer tussle

Al-Hilal open talks to sign Arsenal winger Martinelli

Nick Mashiter, football reporter

What don't Aston Villa need after a raft of star departures this summer?

Ollie Watkins' transfer saga, with Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal trying to sign the striker, leaves Villa looking for a likely replacement with Nicolas Jackson a target.

A winger is also on the agenda while they need a defender after Ezri Konsa's move to Arsenal, and have opened talks for Club Brugge central defender Joel Ordonez after bids for Southampton centre-back Taylor Harwood-Bellis were rejected.

It is clear Aston Villa desperately require a striker more than anything right now.

Although I massively rate Victor Lindelof and Pau Torres, the display against Brighton has worried me slightly.

Therefore, I would welcome another centre-back as well.

It looks like we will be OK in midfield once Johan Manzambi is fit and with the addition of Leon Goretzka.

Watkins' departure would cut deepest - and Villa did not see it coming

Villa in talks with Club Brugge for defender Ordonez

Nizaar Kinsella, football reporter

Bournemouth are used to being picked off and will simply be hoping to come through the final eight days of the transfer window unscathed.

It is clear that big clubs are circling for forward Eli Junior Kroupi and midfielder Alex Scott, who the Cherries insist are not for sale.

In terms of incomings, Bournemouth are largely done as they close in on a move for Juventus goalkeeper Michele Di Gregorio.

Phil McNulty, chief football writer

Brentford are in the fortunate position of being able to choose their deals carefully after some excellent squad strengthening.

The Bees have been looking at left-back, with West Ham's El Hadji Malick Diouf strongly linked, but it hardly seems a matter of urgency with Keane Lewis-Potter able to play as a wing-back with Rico Henry and Aaron Hickey also in the mix.

There is experienced striking cover in the shape of former England international Callum Wilson and an all-round depth to Keith Andrews' squad that was missing last season.

Do not expect it to be a hectic closing few days in the transfer window.

Michael Johnston, Brentford fan

Another forward option - particularly down the left - would take this window for Brentford from a nine to a 10 out of 10.

Mykhailo Mudryk's name has been doing the rounds in recent weeks and Brentford have history there, having chased him prior to his move to Chelsea.

Get someone like Mudryk in, and I don't think the transfer window could've gone much better for Andrews.

It is anticipated Yankuba Minteh will leave for Liverpool, which might create space at Brighton for another forward and Carlos Baleba's exit for Manchester United may see the club make a move for midfield reinforcements.

It is possible there may be other exits but, as usual, Brighton will stick to their data driven recruitment plan.

"We must continue to evolve, invest and innovate while remaining true to the principles that have brought us this far," was chairman Tony Bloom's message to fans before the 4-0 win against Aston Villa.

With Baleba's anticipated departure and Minteh looking likely that he might leave as well, we need to bring a defensive midfielder who can bring a physical presence to our midfield and a winger who is proven at the top level.

We have a lot of games this season with European football, so we need to have the squad depth to compete on all fronts if we want to secure a top-10 finish again.

Nizaar Kinsella, football reporter

Chelsea supporters may want another star forward or a new goalkeeper to replace the unconvincing Robert Sanchez, but Xabi Alonso feels his squad is largely complete for this summer.

However, there is a huge amount of work to do to reduce the squad from 39 players to around 25 within the next eight days. That is the priority, as the Blues will not want frustrated players in their squad this season.

Chelsea need to focus more on the outgoings than incoming players.

With no Europe it's important we do not carry a squad that's too heavy, as we won't have too much room for rotation.

If we were to bring anybody in, I think the priority is a top-drawer goalkeeper.

Nick Mashiter, football reporter

Coventry are in the hunt for Mykhailo Mudryk as the Chelsea winger looks to get his career back on track after serving a 20 month suspension for testing positive for banned substance meldonium.

Defensive cover is also likely to be needed by Frank Lampard while players like Luke Woolfenden could leave on loan.

Honestly, I think we have done enough in the transfer window to build a team that can stay up in this league.

There has been a lot of change at Palace with the loss of Maxence Lacroix and a new manager starting the season in Pierre Sage.

The Eagles have been building depth for their Europa League campaign but still need a few bodies in the building.

Sage has made clear he wants a senior centre-back and Palace could be pushed to sign another defender too after the injury to Chadi Riad in the first game of the Premier League season against Everton.

Ollie Thomas, Crystal Palace fan

Riad's injury has amplified the need for another centre-back who is first-team ready.

Axel Disasi is a good start, but a bigger, permanent move would be great. That, plus a central midfielder, and we are set.

Mateta's contract claim leaves Palace with transfer decision

Phil McNulty, chief football writer

Everton simply must sign a recognised right-back before the window shuts. It has been a glaring problem for more than a year.

It is a weakness recognised by everyone at the club but either a prime target cannot be agreed upon or is out of reach.

Talented midfielder Merlin Rohl took on the job for the opening game against Crystal Palace, while Jake O'Brien and James Garner have also been pressed into service.

Time to finally make a decision and get one in. Maybe David Moyes will also look at adding another striker with questions still hanging over Beto and Thierno Barry.

Chelsea outcast Liam Delap is one name regularly linked with Everton.

Nizaar Kinsella, football reporter

Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa has been clear that he is happy with the club's business so far, but more could be done to make his squad more balanced.

There have been attempts to sign an additional central defender, with a move for Rennes' Abdelhamid Ait Boudlal explored two weeks ago, and that could be a key area the Cottagers look to strengthen.

This is a club that does not operate at the very top end of the transfer market and one that enjoys a deadline-day deal.

It still feels like Fulham need a right winger - whether that is sticking with Oscar Bobb or providing serious competition for him - I think we need to cover for the loss of Harry Wilson's goals.

We also need a right-sided centre-back as there are serious concerns over how Joachim Anderson will fit Arbeloa's new system.

It has already been a busy summer for Hull City's recruitment team but the ambitious Tigers are still working on adding two new forwards in Mohamed Ali-Cho and Ilyas Ansah.

There has also been interest from the club in Real Betis winger Pablo Garcia, although that deal has taken longer than hoped after the La Liga side raised their valuation of the 20-year-old. Stoke City's Sorba Thomas is also a player of interest.

A goalkeeper, midfielder and right-back also could be on the agenda for Sergej Jakirovic's side in the final week of the window.

Over the next week, if we bring in a left winger, one more striker - assuming the Ali-Cho deal also gets completed - a central midfielder, an attacking midfielder and a right-back to add depth and challenge Lewie Coyle for the starting spot, we will be in a strong position to compete.

Nick Mashiter, football reporter

Ipswich have spent over £150m on 12 new signings since returning to the Premier League.

Boss Gary O'Neil expects more, though, and a striker and a midfielder could arrive at Portman Road.

Fringe players like Anis Memeti could leave as O'Neil shapes his squad.

Having pushed the boat out to sign James Trafford from Manchester City, big money signings are probably off the agenda for Leeds in the last week of the window.

They are interested in taking Mykhailo Mudryk on loan but have not been able to strike a deal with the London club as yet as they are looking at other left wingers.

Leeds are also considering back-up options for forwards Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Lukas Nmecha and have also been linked with Frankfurt goalkeeper Michael Zetterer, if Lucas Perri joins Torino on loan as expected.

Leeds have had a great transfer window but they badly need another left-footed left-back as cover for Gabriel Gudmundsson.

Beyond that, perhaps another forward or creative midfielder to contend with Harry Wilson, Brenden Aaronson and Noah Okafor.

As has been the case for most of the summer, Liverpool's priority remains the wide attacking areas and the expectation is that at least one and maybe two wingers will come in over the coming week.

Andoni Iraola said that personnel was not the issue when it came to defensive midfielders, the manner in which his side conceded twice at Newcastle would suggest that it would be wise to address Liverpool's deficiencies in that department.

Nahyan Chowdhury, Liverpool fan

It is no secret Liverpool have been actively looking in the market for wingers - Bradley Barcola, Ibrahim Mbaye and Yankuba Minteh - and Sunday's display against Newcastle cemented that with Rio Ngumoha looking uncomfortable on the right.

However, the performance also showed Liverpool may need a defensive midfielder to plug the huge disconnect between the defence and midfield, especially on the counter attack.

Liverpool fans have been crying out for a Fabinho replacement since his departure, but it could be too late with a week to go.

Does Elliott have a Liverpool future after latest omission?

Shamoon Hafez, football reporter

Manchester City could well be one of the busiest sides to do business in the remaining days of the transfer window.

With Savinho gone and Omar Marmoush and Nico Gonzalez seemingly on their way out, there will be gaps in the squad which will need addressing.

A deal for Ayyoub Bouaddi has been agreed with Lille, and with Palmeiras for winger Allan, while BBC Sport has been told winger Pedro Neto remains of interest and speculation around signing Chelsea team-mate Enzo Fernandez continues.

Director of football Hugo Viana may have his hands full in these coming days.

Steven McInerney, Manchester City fan

City need numbers. We have let go of so many players, with Omar Marmoush and maybe Nico Gonzalez set to follow Rodri and Savinho out of the door alongside several others this summer.

It is essential that City bring in three or four new names before the deadline, with two of them being midfielders.

The maths whizz turned £86m teenage star heading to Man City

Man City agree deal for Palmeiras winger Allan

Carlos Baleba's arrival completes the midfield recruitment, now all eyes are on the left-back situation and whether Manchester United bring in someone to compete with Luke Shaw.

The club has a long-standing interest in Newcastle's Lewis Hall, but are also assessing Barcelona's Alejandro Balde and have been heavily linked with Jorge Salinas of Racing Santander.

It is also possible they bring in another forward but that probably depends on one of their existing ones leaving, with Joshua Zirkzee the most likely.

Jay Motty, Manchester United fan

A left-back is essential and this is not just a knee-jerk reaction to the defeat at Hull City - you can see United are short in that position.

We can not realistically expect Luke Shaw to play every game this season and there are still doubts as to whether Michael Carrick trusts Patrick Dorgu in defence.

Baleba completes £70m Man Utd move from Brighton

Man Utd's midfield spending is done - now for a left-back?

Ciaran Kelly, football reporter

Newcastle United's young signings did not look fazed when they faced Liverpool on their Premier League debuts at the weekend.

Manager Matthias Jaissle could still use another midfielder with some top-flight nous, though, after Newcastle sold Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali, and the club are progressing with a move for Manchester City's Nico Gonzalez.

Beyond that, bringing in a mobile and versatile forward who could chip in would help ease the burden on William Osula and Yoane Wissa.

Nick Mashiter, football reporter

Nottingham Forest are still working on deals after only bringing in three new faces so far this summer.

A striker and a full-back would be ideal with the club in talks for Chelsea's Liam Delap, while Fiorentina right-back Dodo is of interest.

Boss Oliver Glasner has played down the need for midfield reinforcements, despite Elliot Anderson's departure to Manchester City.

Forest working on deal for Chelsea striker Delap

With the signings of French full-back Dayann Methalie from Toulouse and Antwerp midfielder Jules Ahoka over the line, the obvious position Sunderland still need to fill is right wing.

Sporting's Geny Catamo is the name most heavily linked.

Asked about reported interest from the Premier League, Sporting boss Rui Borges insisted Catamo is "happy" at the Portuguese club, but we have seen before that does not necessarily mean much.

Given Eliezer Mayenda has left, meaning Brian Brobbey and Wilson Isidor are the club's only first-team strikers, another forward who plays through the middle is probably needed.

Phil McNulty, chief football writer

Spurs have strengthened by spending heavily in the summer, but if Dominic Solanke is not going to be used regularly as a main striker, then this is where Roberto de Zerbi must look next.

Richarlison took the starting role in the opening weekend loss at Brentford, and while a deal for Manchester City's Omar Marmoush is progressing, is this actually his best role?

Tottenham desperately need forward players who can turn De Zerbi's quick attacks into decisive moments.

Currently Spurs have the players to play through pressure but don't have the players to maximise the situations this creates.

A winger and a striker who can improve us will be a drastic upgrade.

title: Sir Billy Boston - 'the world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
description: Rugby league commentator Matt Newsum says Sir Billy Boston was a "world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told".
fullText:
When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.

For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.

Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.

You can tell the importance of someone by how many statues have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.

His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.

Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.

Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club.

Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.

Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.

It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.

£3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.

This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".

The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance.

Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.

Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.

Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.

He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.

Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.

Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.

It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.

Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community.

He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.

Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.

There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.

His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

title: Trump plans to grow his way out of $40 trillion debt crisis—it’s a ‘fantastic story’ but virtually impossible, says top budget economist
description: "If you tell the debt markets: 'Hey, we think we're gonna be able to grow our way out of this,' and then a year later they're not seeing any improvements from that, then it's a credibility issue."
fullText:
The U.S. national debt has hit $40 trillion, and the Trump administration is facing questions about its budget plans as a result. The good news is, there has one: The American economy will apparently grow its way out of any fiscal crisis.

"It's been a problem for 35 years," Trump told reporters Friday. "And what we have now … is we have tremendous growth. And the way you take care of debt is with growth, and we have tremendous growth. We've never had growth like we have right now."

"There's nothing magic about the $40 trillion number," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC last week, "And we can grow our way out of that."

Economists would be inclined to agree with Bessent: The value of the debt, while an extraordinary milestone, doesn't hold much relative weight. What economists (and more importantly, the bond market) is watching is the debt-to-GDP ratio: This demonstrates the level of borrowing by a country against its economic capacity to repay and service it.

Currently, the U.S. ratio stands at 122%. To bring it back into a lower balance, an economy could cut its borrowing or—as Bessent suggests—increase its growth.

When the alternative is cutting borrowing and, as a result, government spending, the growth plan is a more optimistic and politically palatable route.

It's also the latest in a series of solutions proposed by the White House: Originally, President Trump had suggested that tariffs would pay down the national debt (the plan was quickly nixed by a Supreme Court ruling ordering the administration to repay approximately $100 billion in revenues that the justices deemed illegal).

Trump later suggested a "golden visa" strategy—selling rich immigrants visas at $5 million each—could pay down the national debt. The policies were novel, but economists broadly welcomed action by the Trump Administration on the fiscal picture.

But now there a bond market reckoning looming. The risk premium demanded by investors for holding the 30-year Treasury rose to over 5.3% in recent days, prompting U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to deploy $4 billion or 

So, can the U.S. grow its way out of debt? It's a "fantastic story," says Kent Smetters, Boettner Professor of economics and public policy at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania.

Unfortunately, Professor Smetters—the faculty director of a fiscal analysis tool called the Penn Wharton Budget Model—says the plan is also "pretty clearly" not feasible. He explained in an interview with Fortune: "People often get the causality kind of opposite. They think more growth, less of a debt problem, and in reality, it's just the opposite … We deal with the debt issue in order to try to aid economic growth, not vice versa."

title: A British Army commander testing war robots says they aren't always the right tool for the job
description: Uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, can present logistics, power, navigation, and control challenges for soldiers, he said.
fullText:
A British Army commander says ground robots can be useful but come with drawbacks.

UGVs can create logistics, power, navigation, and control challenges for troops.

Ukraine shows their value may be mainly in dangerous, specialized missions that protect soldiers.

The commander of a British Army battalion tasked with experimenting with new technologies said that his unit has tested out dozens of ground robots. He concluded that they can be useful, but only for certain missions. And they come with a long list of challenges.

As Western militaries rush to absorb lessons from the war in Ukraine and integrate more uncrewed systems into their respective forces, soldiers are finding that some systems might look good on paper but aren't effective in all combat scenarios.

Ground robots, in particular, can face weight, navigation, cost, and power constraints that raise questions about when and how they should be used. In Ukraine's case, the systems have seen use in logistics operations, replacing soldiers in highly dangerous areas of the battlefield, but soldiers have also said they're not a catch-all solution.

At a recent US Army-led exercise at Fort Irwin in California, a handful of American allies and partners gathered with US forces to experiment with new systems in a simulated conflict against a near-peer adversary. The British Army's experimentation unit, the 2nd Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, was present for the event alongside the unit that will take over their experimentation role, the 1st Battalion Irish Guards.

During the recent exercise, Lt. Col. John Black, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, told Business Insider that he and his unit have seen and tested a wide range of uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs.

"Any use case you can think of, we've tried it," he said, adding that they're not just driving it around to see how it works; rather, they are focused on "trying to employ it in a tactical scenario."

Through that experimentation, Black and his troops have encountered problems that can make UGVs difficult to use. For instance, many of the medium- to large-sized UGVs they tested required trailers or flatbed trucks to transport. Depending on how soldiers are moving and what they're carrying, that creates a logistical burden.

And once they've moved it into position, troops still have to figure out how to get it into the fight.

"Even if they've got quite long range and good speed, there's still going to be a process where you're moving them into the fight," Black said.

UGVs can also create power and refueling challenges. Depending on the system, specifically it's size, range, and capabilities, troops in the field may need to carry extra batteries, generators, or fuel — or periodically bring the robot back to a charging point.

Remote control introduces another set of problems, from maintaining a reliable connection to keeping the robot on course. The systems can also struggle with difficult terrain.

Often, their advertised range doesn't translate cleanly to real-world conditions, such as uneven ground. Obstacles "confound" most UGVs, Black said.

Whether UGVs can rely on autonomous features is a particularly thorny subject. Autonomy has become a major area of interest across uncrewed capabilities, but Black said some manufacturers have moved away from offering autonomous UGVs.

"We have seen, over the last few years, these vendors stop offering autonomous ones because it's unworkable," he said, explaining that such autonomous features can result in the system being more expensive and difficult to use.

Despite those limitations, Black said there are certain situations where he sees value, including breaches and mine removal.

Both missions are incredibly dangerous for soldiers. For that reason, militaries have been using remote-controlled technologies for breaching fortified positions and removing mines for decades. Certain UGVs coming online now could be the next evolution in that technology, but other methods could prove more practical.

Ground robots are seeing growing use in Ukraine, sometimes operating as a safer option than sending soldiers into "the kill zone" to deliver supplies and ammo. Ukraine has also used them offensively, such as driving one equipped with a gun off a drone boat in a first-of-its-kind robotic amphibious assault.

However, their growing use in that fight hasn't settled the debate on their overall usefulness. Black indicated that they might be a niche tool, most effective only in those cases where keeping a soldier out of harm's way matters most.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Meta billionaire Mark Zuckerberg has just bought a 196-year-old Gothic castle with 11 bedrooms in Ireland worth up to $35 million
description: Just like hedge fund mogul Ken Griffin, the Meta CEO has joined the list of ultrarich Americans buying up multimillion-dollar mansions in Europe.
fullText:
Wealthy Americans living in luxe California mansions and New York penthouses are now snatching up historic homes abroad. Mark Zuckerberg, the billionaire CEO of Meta, just added a 196-year-old Gothic castle in Ireland to his growing property portfolio.

Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, recently bought the Strancally Castle in Waterford, Ireland: a 19th-century, Gothic-style mansion overlooking the River Blackwater in the southeast.

The three-story home was built in 1830 and later extensively renovated in 2003, reportedly featuring 11 main bedrooms, a cut-stone Gothic Revival facade, 16,000 square feet of living space, and sprawling green lawns across its 440 acres. While the transaction was not listed on the Irish state property price register, the Irish Times estimates that the billionaire couple's new home could be worth between €20 million (around $23.3 million) and €30 million (roughly $35 million).

Beyond luxury and historic appeal, there could also be a practical purpose behind Zuckerberg's purchase. Meta's international headquarters are nestled in Dublin, about 125 miles from Strancally Castle. The family won't reside in the Emerald Isle full-time, but the estate will serve as a European home base for the highly influential family. The Waterford City and County Council also emphasized the area's rugged coastlines and picturesque towns when asked about the billionaire's castle purchase.

"Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters," Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg, tells Fortune.

Zuckerberg is just one of many wealthy Americans adding foreign postcodes to their property portfolios.

In 2019, hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin bought a $122 million Georgian mansion near Buckingham Palace—which, at the time, was London's most expensive sale in over a decade. The 16,000-square-foot mansion located at 3 Carlton Gardens boasts a spa and indoor swimming pool, as well as a historic backstory, having previously served as Charles de Gaulle's wartime headquarters.

Other ultrarich Americans including George Clooney, Tom Ford, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt have all added European homes to their portfolios.

More wealthy, non-famous Americans have been eyeing up U.K. homes as well, chasing stability as the U.S. grapples with soaring cost of living, political polarization, and economic uncertainty.

title: Mike Lindell misses deadline for recount payment, seeks restraining order
description: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the...
fullText:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the state's gubernatorial primaries.

His campaign said in a statement that Simon's office had put Lindell "in an untenable position" by placing restrictions on his proposed audit — limiting the recount to just the two leading Republican candidates.

Lindell lost the election to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) by roughly 11 percentage points, according to Decision Desk HQ. But the MyPillow founder refused to concede, later claiming there were irregularities in vote totals.

"The rest of the candidates' vote would not be counted under their contingent plan. Nor would the Democrat ballots be recounted," Lindell's campaign wrote Monday.

"Why is this important?" it continued. "In addition to being a violation of Minnesota state law, the anomalies on election night reporting identified by Mike Lindell's team show an algorithm that applies to ALL of the candidates not simply Lindell and Demuth."

Cassondra Knudson, a spokesperson for Simon, told The Hill that the office did not receive a payment or a discretionary request by the Aug. 24 deadline. She added that, at this time, the state does not plan to conduct a recount for the Aug. 11 primary.

In its statement, Lindell's campaign attached an authorization form appearing to show an $825,000 transaction in progress as proof of "wire transfer readiness" for the potential audit, dated Monday morning.

The campaign is now asking the state officials to waive the Monday deadline until a court can rule on the alleged Minnesota law violations.

Knudson said that "next steps" for Lindell's legal action against Simon and the Minnesota State Canvassing Board for their handling of the recount processes "will be decided by the court."

"Our office provided the contingent recount plan to Mr. Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on August 18. The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans," she said.

The MyPillow founder currently owes the electronic voting system company Smartmatic $56,369 in sanctions following a defamation lawsuit — which his attorneys say he cannot afford. Lindell accused the company in several media appearances of rigging the 2020 presidential election, echoing President Trump's similar false claims.

On Aug. 19, Lindell's lawyers sent a letter to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan to file a motion to reconsider the ruling holding him liable for defamation.

title: Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds
description:
Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running
The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.
Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Exclusive: Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire sites predicted to emit 4.5m tonnes a year when fully running

The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.

Experts have said this demonstrates the “serious threat” datacentres pose to the UK’s legally binding climate goals.

Analysis by the non-profit group Foxglove reveals that when fully operational, the Wapseys Wood datacentre in Buckinghamshire and the Quest Park datacentre in Bedfordshire will use 1.3GW of power and will produce more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions.

ExxonMobil emitted 3.9m tonnes in 2023, according to the global energy thinktank Ember.

AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are currently 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.

Because of the long wait to connect to the grid, the Wapseys Wood and Quest Park datacentres are seeking to build their own on-site gas-fired power stations.

Based on government figures on the carbon intensity of electricity generation, Foxglove has calculated these projects will produce 4.577m tonnes of carbon emissions per year.

A government spokesperson said these figures were “misleading” because of the assumption that both projects will run at 100% utilisation from day one, which they said was “not accurate”.

Tom Hegarty, head of communications at Foxglove, said assuming a 100% utilisation rate followed standard industry practice.

Kierra Box, a trade and environmental regulation campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said the aim was for datacentres to increase load and run at full capacity, and so it was “valid to look at those top level predictions”.

The former England and Wales Green party leader Caroline Lucas described the projected emissions from these projects as “absolutely horrifying”, and said it should be ringing alarm bells right across government.

The government says its own analysis shows there are multiple pathways for this rapid datacentre rollout to fit within the seventh carbon budget, which sets out how the government will reach its international climate targets.

However there remains a high level of uncertainty over how this will work.

Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, which is leading an inquiry into the environmental impact of datacentres, said this analysis was a “potent reminder that without the right measures in place, data centres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals”.

Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said the two projects were “catastrophic for our carbon budgets”. He said the only way the rapid rollout of datacentres could fit within these budgets was if other elements of the economy were given much stricter carbon budgets.

Sam Hunter-Jones, a ClientEarth lawyer, said every megawatt powering a datacentre connected to the grid was a megawatt that could not be used to replace fossil fuels elsewhere. “The reality is that unchecked datacentre growth is making the transition away from fossil fuels harder, not easier,” he said.

The datacentres are two of the first to be fast-tracked through the government’s nationally significant infrastructure project (NSIP) regime. This regime allows developers to rapidly deliver infrastructure projects by bypassing local planning authorities with decisions instead handled by central government.

Hayes said it was a “very worrying sign” that the government had allowed two gas-fired datacentres to apply into the NSIP regime. “I think that sends an extremely bad signal and demonstrates that they are not serious about addressing the emissions associated with datacentres,” he said, describing it as an “affront to local people”.

Lucas also raised concerns about the projects being fast-tracked, and said it “insulates” them from local scrutiny.

“In order to be able to make sensible decisions on which projects should go ahead and where they should be, we need to have more information in the public domain. We need to have more scrutiny, not less, and yet things like the NSIP regime are moving things in the opposite direction,” she said.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Datacentres are a vital part of our economy and our everyday lives, helping us interact with the services we need, while driving growth and renewal for communities. We will enable the development and growth of new industries, such as datacentres, by building unprecedented amounts of clean power.”

Wapseys Wood declined to comment. Quest Park did not respond to a request for comment.

title: A Pocket Full of Slagford – a retro-futurist take on Thatcher-era northern England
description:
Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north
Something is amiss in the dingy town of Slagford, and curious scamp Pip Bunting is the only one who can find out what. So quit your mithering, it’s time to discover just how grim it truly is up north.

fullText:
Developer Patrick Grant was born in Australia and lives in New Zealand, but a childhood of British TV inspired him to set a comedy game in a bleak vision of the north

Something is amiss in the dingy town of Slagford, and curious scamp Pip Bunting is the only one who can find out what. So quit your mithering, it’s time to discover just how grim it truly is up north.

A Pocket Full of Slagford is an upcoming retro-styled 3D puzzle adventure game set in a surreal alternative-reality near-future northern England that never escaped the clutches of Thatcherism. The story follows the misadventures of a young local lad from the eponymous Slagford after he takes ownership of a mysterious relic that lets him wreak havoc on reality.

It’s the passion project of Australia-born, New Zealand-based artist Patrick Grant, who formed solo-developer studio Slumps to create a game inspired by the point-and-click classics from the late 80s and early 90s, such as LucasArts’ catalogue and Grim Fandango.

“They’re just a great format for narrative-heavy games, like an interactive story,” says Grant. “I like designing puzzles as well, so I always wanted to make a point-and-click. But from playing a lot, I know how samey they can be. From the start I was thinking about what I could do differently.”

The result of Grant’s prototyping is what he describes as a “jigsaw sticker book kind of thing.” As you navigate the nasty industrial hellscape, you collect imprints of the game’s scenery. If, along the way, you spot a place where these imprints align, you can paste them into the world to solve puzzles. Grant is also committed to evoking the oft-forgotten CD-Rom era of the late ’90s, complete with looping CG-rendered backgrounds and janky 3D models with far too many sharp edges.

Yet he’s keen to emphasise that his main focus is the narrative. While the trailer and Steam store page feature a fair few Yorkshire-isms, A Pocket Full of Slagford’s story and dialogue take inspiration from various aspects of northern English culture, despite Grant admitting to having never actually spent any real time in the area.

“In the colonies we get a lot of BBC English programming,” he explains. “So when I was growing up there was so much British telly that I’d be watching. There’s this BBC miniseries from the 80s called Boys from the Blackstuff, about this group of scousers getting up to mischief, set in the Thatcher years, just trying to make ends meet. It’s incredibly well written – this mix of sad and funny – against that whole big economic collapse. I got interested in that, reading about the Thatcher years.”

That interest is what inspired A Pocket Full of Slagford’s bleak setting. While Grant says he wasn’t trying to make a political point when he went into the project, he’s not shying away from the issues of the time: “Because of that working-class setting, you end up naturally touching on points like the wealth disparity, which I show in the game, and the class conflict. Specifically, from watching stuff like Boys from the Blackstuff, or Billy Elliot, I was interested in the infighting that goes on within these classes.”

Despite touching on these themes, Grant stresses that he’s going for a comedic, surrealist angle. As he puts it: “I was like, what if I set it in the future and, instead of coal, they’re mining shit out of the ground?” He may not be trying to make a political statement about Thatcherism, but some might say he has hit on an apt analogy.

title: Trump says Strait of Hormuz has been demined, warns Iran not to plant more

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the United ‌States, through its ⁠Space Force, was watching "every square inch" of the Strait, a key waterway ⁠in the global energy supply chain.

"There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in ​full ​force and effect," Trump ​said.

The U.S. and ‌Iran have not conducted air strikes on each other's militaries for weeks, but attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued as the two sides vie for control ‌of the narrow maritime passage.
